docs.title: PocketCW
docs.text:
PocketCW is open-source replacement firmware for the HamCube Morse code trainer. The Mini and the Pro run the same firmware, so PocketCW runs on both. The Pro adds a decoder board that listens to a radio. PocketCW is free software under the GPL-3.0-or-later license.

PocketCW is not affiliated with HamCube or Nintendo.

docs.title: What it does
docs.text:
• An iambic keyer that also works with a straight key or a sideswiper, with a live decode of what you send.
  • A timing tape and histograms that show how close your keying is to standard timing.
  • Receive drills: Koch groups, common words, callsigns, and full ragchew QSOs to copy.
  • QSO practice: activate a park or a summit and work a pileup, or hunt activators.
  • Four memories that key your radio, with repeat for calling CQ.
  • Copy accuracy per character, your most common mixups, and practice history.
  • A USB keyboard mode that types what you key, or keys VBand.

PocketCW was tested on a Mini with board version 2.64. Other boards from 2.60 and the Pro may work, but nobody has tried them yet.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• Rust from rustup, version 1.88 or later. The code uses let chains, from the 2024 edition.
  • The target for the AT32F403A, a Cortex-M4F:
rustup target add thumbv7em-none-eabihf
  • The LLVM tools. mkimage.sh takes llvm-objcopy and llvm-objdump from the rustup toolchain folder.
rustup component add llvm-tools
  • To flash from macOS: clang from the Xcode command line tools. tools/panic.sh uses their lldb.

docs.title: Build the image
docs.text:
sh tools/mkimage.sh

The script builds firmware/ in release mode and writes firmware/target/A000014.bin. firmware/.cargo/config.toml sets the target, so a plain cargo build in firmware/ also builds for the device.

The script stops with an error in two cases:

  • The image does not start at 0x08005000. The bootloader is below that address. See Flash layout.
  • The image is larger than 236 KB, the app area.

At the end, the script prints the command that flashes the image.

The linker script firmware/memory.x puts the app at 0x08005000, with 236 KB of flash and 64 KB of RAM. Its .fast_text section holds the sample interrupt, inside the flash that has no wait states. See MCU. firmware/build.rs passes the nmagic option to the linker. Without it, the linker maps the ELF headers at 0x08000000, inside the bootloader, and mkimage.sh refuses the image.

docs.title: Flash the image
docs.text:
The device installs updates through its bootloader, which shows a USB drive. macOS must not mount that drive. See Flash layout for the reason.

  1. Build the install tool once. mkimage.sh prints a command that runs it from tools/:
clang -O2 -arch arm64 -arch x86_64 -mmacosx-version-min=10.15 -o tools/pocketcw-flash tools/pocketcw-flash.c -framework DiskArbitration -framework CoreFoundation
  1. Run the command that mkimage.sh printed:
tools/pocketcw-flash firmware/target/A000014.bin
  1. Follow the steps the tool prints. macOS asks for your Mac login password, because the tool writes to the raw disk through authopen.

pocketcw-flash refuses a file that would write below 0x08005000, or past the end of the 256 KB flash. The install guide and troubleshooting pages cover the steps on the device.

docs.title: Test
docs.text:
The tests run on your computer:

cd logic
cargo test

logic/ has no target setting, so it builds for your computer. The firmware crate has no tests.

docs.title: Panic screen
docs.text:
A panic shows up to six return addresses, from the call into panic_fmt outward. Give them to tools/panic.sh, which names each function, inlined calls included, with its file and line:

sh tools/panic.sh 0801382D 08024A11 08031F05

The first frame outside core:: is the code that panicked. The function is exact; the line can be off where the compiler merged identical panic paths. FFFFFFF9 and the like mark an exception entry: the frames after it are the callers of the function the interrupt stopped. That function itself is not shown.

The script reads the last app build. For a release, tools/release.sh keeps the ELF in symbols/A000014-VERSION.elf; pass it with -e.

docs.title: Hardware probe
docs.text:
firmware/src/bin/probe.rs is a separate image for checking a board. It shows the chip and board IDs, reads the LCD memory back, scans the I2C bus, shows the live inputs, and tests the audio codec, the PA8 audio output and standby.

sh tools/mkimage.sh probe

The probe image also goes to firmware/target/A000014.bin. Flash it the same way, and flash the app again after.

docs.title: USB probe
docs.text:
firmware/src/bin/usbprobe.rs is a separate image for checking the USB device. It shows up on the computer as a USB keyboard and serial port named "PocketCW USB probe".

sh tools/mkimage.sh usbprobe
Input Sends Dit contact (tip) Holds Left Ctrl, as VBand reads a dit. Dah contact (ring) Holds Right Ctrl, as VBand reads a dah. F1 Types cq test de pocketcw and Enter. Hold the dial 1.5 s Turns the device off.

The screen shows the clock source, the USB state, the bus reset count, and the reports the computer took. CONFIGURED means the computer accepted the keyboard. macOS may open its Keyboard Setup Assistant the first time; close it.

The image goes to firmware/target/A000014.bin. Flash it the same way, and flash the app again after.

docs.title: Content pack
docs.text:
The content pack is F000400.bin: the words for the drills, with clips of the Kokoro voice af_heart at 8789 Hz (tools/pack/voices/kokoro-af_heart). logic/src/pack.rs gives the format. The entries come from three lists:

  • tools/pack/words/chars.txt: every character Morse sends, so the device can spell a word the pack lacks or spells, such as QTH.
  • tools/pack/words/ham.txt: CW words, abbreviations, Q codes and prosigns, each with the text the voice says and, for an abbreviation, its meaning. A word said letter by letter, such as QTH with the said "Q T H", gets no clip: the device spells it from the character clips, so a letter's fix applies in every spelled word. Its said must spell its text, without the brackets of a prosign. A meaning gets a clip, "location", which the device says after the word when the word is on its own, as in drills.
  • tools/pack/words/common.txt: English words from the top 3177 of wordfreq. tools/pack/wordlist.py writes it, leaving out the words in tools/pack/words/blocklist.txt: offensive words, fragments, and words seldom sent in a CW contact. The blocklist is reviewed down to that rank, so raising the rank means reviewing the new words first. It needs the wordfreq package, and runs only when the list changes. The pack takes the most frequent of them that fit in one update file, 8,372,224 bytes.

docs.title: Voice tools
docs.text:
The voice tools need Python 3.12, since they encode with audioop, which Python 3.13 removed, and espeak-ng 1.52 or later and ffmpeg on the path (brew install python@3.12 espeak-ng ffmpeg on macOS). tools/pack/setup.py makes a venv in tools/pack/.venv with the packages in tools/pack/requirements.txt, and downloads the model files each voice names into tools/pack/models, about 350 MB. It checks each file's sha256. Run it again after a change to either:

python3.12 tools/pack/setup.py

Each folder in tools/pack/voices is one voice, with three files:

  • voice.toml: the engine, the voice, its speed, and the model files with their URLs and sha256.
  • fixes.txt: what the voice says for a clip, over the said or meaning column of the word lists, as a respelling or as phonemes between slashes. A fix belongs to one voice: a respelling that fixes one voice can break another.
  • review.txt: the marks tools/pack/audition.py gives each clip.

docs.title: Building the pack
docs.text:
tools/pack/pack.py builds the pack. It keeps what the voice says for each phoneme string in firmware/target/clip-cache/speech, about 115 MB, and each finished clip beside it under a key of what makes it: tools/pack/voiceclips.py, the ffmpeg version and CLIP_RECIPE in tools/pack/pack.py. cargo clean deletes both. A rebuild speaks only text whose phonemes are new: a change to voice.toml or to kokoro-onnx speaks every clip again, and an espeak-ng upgrade only the words it changes. A change to how clips are made, such as their level, makes every clip again from the saved speech in about 4 minutes. The first build speaks every clip, in about 15 minutes. It prints how many clips have a mark for the speech they have now:

tools/pack/.venv/bin/python tools/pack/pack.py --out firmware/target/pack

How each clip is made, in tools/pack/voiceclips.py and tools/pack/pack.py:

  • Kokoro gets phonemes in the form of misaki, the tool its training data went through. espeak-ng makes the phonemes, and a table from misaki's espeak fallback converts them. Without the table, vowels sound foreign: "bee" comes out like "beay".
  • A character ends in a period, and so does each part of a word that mixes letters and words: "C W ops" goes to the voice as "C. W. ops.". Kokoro rushes a lone letter and runs spelled letters together; as the end of a sentence it says each in full. Kokoro pauses up to about 225 ms after each period, so in a clip whose phonemes end a sentence and go on, every pause longer than 50 ms is cut to 50 ms, a comma's too. A part that already ends in a mark, such as "Q. T H", gets no second one.
  • A meaning ends in a period too, and its commas become ellipses: Kokoro barely pauses at a comma, and "prosign… over" sounds right where "prosign, over" runs together. The device plays it 200 ms after the word; with the silence at the clips' ends, that is about the pause Kokoro makes after a sentence.
  • A clip whose phonemes start with s or f starts at the hiss. Kokoro often says a short vowel before it, so "sports" came out as "ehsports" and "fast" like "vast". A 10 ms frame hisses when it has more power above 3.5 kHz than from 100 Hz to 1.5 kHz; 20 to 100 ms of voiced sound before the first hiss is cut, and the clip fades in over 5 ms. A longer lead is the word itself: "fist" has no hiss at its f.
  • Before encoding, a treble boost undoes the loss of the device's straight-line upsampling, 6 dB at the top of the band.
  • Then the speech level is set to 7 dB under the sidetone's, from the power of its 20 ms frames without the pauses. A limiter keeps the peaks under 0.8 of full scale: ADPCM overshot dense peaks by up to 16% in a test. The synth plays 0.8 at the sidetone's peak (CLIP_CEILING in logic/src/synth.rs). A clip scaled by its peak alone sounds about 11 dB under the sidetone, since speech has short peaks far above its level. The build prints the level of the clips against the sidetone's.

docs.title: Reviewing the clips
docs.text:
tools/pack/audition.py plays each clip as the device plays it: the clip from the cache, decoded and upsampled the way logic/src/adpcm.rs does it. Build the pack first, so every clip is in the cache. Then:

tools/pack/.venv/bin/python tools/pack/audition.py
  1. Mark. The list shows the clips to review, and each plays when it comes up. Good and Bad mark the clip, and the next clip plays; with the list focused, G and B do the same. N goes to the note: type what is wrong, and Enter marks the clip bad. Space plays it again, and Up and Down move. Each mark goes to review.txt at once, so you can stop at any clip.
  2. Fix. Pick Bad in the filter. For each clip, type a respelling the voice reads more clearly, such as boy see for BOISE, and press Enter to hear it. A word's respelling with a lone capital letter or digit gets its periods as "C W ops" does, and is still a clip of its own. The phonemes field shows these periods, so phonemes edited from it keep them. When no respelling does it, edit the phonemes instead. They are misaki phonemes, the form Kokoro is given, and a character Kokoro does not know is an error. The phoneme keys under the field type the ones a keyboard lacks, each with a word it sounds in; Kokoro takes ɡ, not g. To stress a word, give it ˈ before its stressed vowel and take the stress off its neighbors, or mark its pitch: tə ↗jˈu ↘Onli puts the weight on "you". Play kept plays the clip the pack has now. Keep fix writes the fix to fixes.txt and marks the clip good; Reset puts back the word list's said, and Keep fix then drops the fix.
  3. Check. A fix is for one clip: a word's fix leaves its meaning as it is, and a character's fix changes every word the device spells with it. Build the pack again: a kept fix is already in the cache. Install it and spot check on the device speaker with say.

A mark is for the speech it was given on. When the speech changes, because of a fix, a new model or an espeak-ng upgrade that changes the phonemes, the mark shows as stale until you mark the clip again.

docs.title: Listening packs
docs.text:
tools/pack/listenpack.py builds a small pack that compares ways of making clips, to judge them on the device speaker. Each test word is made each way, as words such as QTHA and QTHB. The ways at lower rates go through what the device does to them, so the pack plays at 17,578 Hz with firmware of its pack format.

--no-voice builds the words without clips, in a second. --fixture logic/fixtures/pack.bin writes the small pack the logic tests read; build it again after a format change.

Install it, then speak a word over the serial port:

tools/pocketcw-flash firmware/target/pack/F000400.bin

python3 -I tools/pocketcw.py info say QTH say "hello K5MME 73"

INFO gives PACK= and the word count, or NONE, OLD or BAD. At startup the device checks the word list's CRC, and not the clips', which take too long to read.

docs.title: Voice probe
docs.text:
firmware/src/bin/voiceprobe.rs plays spoken words through PA8, so you can score by ear whether a voice is clear enough. Each image holds one voice: 20 words at 8789 Hz and 20 at 5859 Hz, the 17,578 Hz sample rate divided by 2 and 3. It also times the synth's heaviest load against the sample period, and shows it as SYNTH worst/4096 MEAN n in CPU cycles.

tools/pack/voiceclips.py builds the clips, with the voice tools. Piper also needs piper-tts and en_US-ljspeech-high.onnx, which setup.py does not install. Then build the image with the clip folder in VOICE_CLIPS:

tools/pack/.venv/bin/python tools/pack/voiceclips.py kokoro --models tools/pack/models --out firmware/target/voice-kokoro

VOICE_CLIPS=$PWD/firmware/target/voice-kokoro sh tools/mkimage.sh voiceprobe

Without VOICE_CLIPS, the image builds with no clips and says so.

Control Action F1 Plays the next word, with its text hidden. F2 Plays the word again. F3 Shows the word. F1 or F4, with the word shown Scores it right or wrong. Dial click Switches the rate. Dial turn Volume. Hold the dial 1.5 s Turns the device off.

A rate passes at 19 of 20 right. Flash the app again after.

docs.title: SPI flash probe
docs.text:
firmware/src/bin/flashprobe.rs reads the 16 MB SPI flash beside the screen. At start it only reads: the JEDEC ID, the status registers and write protection, the SFDP table (size, page size, erase types and times), F000400.bin at 0x100000 at 18 MHz and at 4.5 MHz, and a scan of every 4 KB sector that lists the used ranges.

It erases and programs only in the log range, 0xC00000 to 0xDFFFFF, since the driver refuses writes anywhere else, and only sectors that read blank or that carry its own tags.

Control Action F1 Erase and program test in two blank sectors from 0xD00000: erase times, page program time, a page written in 16 pieces, read back, then erased again. F2 Writes a PCWMARK tag in each marker sector that reads blank: at each end of the log range. F3 Shows whether each marker is still there, then scans again. F4, twice Erases every sector in the log range that starts with a PCWMARK or PCWTEST tag. Hold the dial 1.5 s Turns the device off.

The bootloader test shows what installing an F file erases past the file's end. tools/flashtest.py writes a 2 MB F000400.bin with every 4 KB sector tagged PCWTEST:

python tools/flashtest.py --out firmware/target/flashtest

sh tools/mkimage.sh flashprobe
  1. Build and flash the probe. Read the scan, then press F1, then F2.
  2. Flash firmware/target/flashtest/F000400.bin.
  3. Turn the device on and press F3. The tags line counts the test sectors.
  4. Press F4 twice, then flash dist/F000400.bin from tools/release.sh and the app.

docs.title: Pop probe
docs.text:
Finds which ES8388 write makes a volume change pop in silence. Each mode toggles one kind of write, by hand with F4 or once a second with F3, so the pops can be compared by ear. A pop with SAME VALUES or READ ONLY comes from the bus traffic, not a gain change.

sh tools/mkimage.sh popprobe

docs.title: Remote control and screenshots
docs.text:
tools/pocketcw.py drives the device over USB serial. It presses the buttons, keys and plays text, shows what the device decodes and plays, reads and changes settings, saves the screen as a PNG, and saves the stats and the key timing as CSV. It needs Python 3 on macOS or Linux, with no other packages. Serial interface describes the commands and the event lines.

  1. Set USB OUT to SERIAL, so the device is on USB and types nothing.
  2. Plug the device into the computer.
  3. Run the steps, such as:
python3 -I tools/pocketcw.py F4 RIGHT CLICK shot timing.png
Step Does F1 to F4, LEFT, RIGHT, CLICK Presses and releases that button. LEFT and RIGHT turn the dial one step. hold F1 to hold F4 Holds that F button past its hold time, then releases it. shot FILE.png Saves the screen. wait MS Pauses, for a screen that changes on its own. send TEXT Keys the text and waits until it is sent, then shows what the device decoded. Put text with spaces in quotes. expect REGEX Waits up to 60 s for an event line that matches from its start, such as expect "PLAY ". listen MS Shows the event lines that arrive in that time. shots DIR Saves every screen into the folder. See Every screen. manual Saves every screen for the user manual. See The manual's screenshots. info Shows the firmware version, the screen and the panel. get NAME Shows a setting or memory, such as get SPEED. get all shows every one. set NAME VALUE Changes a setting or memory, written as the screen writes it, such as set MODE "IAMBIC A". play TEXT Sounds the text as a receive drill does, and waits until it ends. stop Stops what send and play started. stats letters FILE.csv Saves each Koch character's tries, percent right, mastery, and whether it is in play. Shows the mixups. stats progress FILE.csv Saves each practice session. edges MS FILE.csv Saves each change on the key and paddle lines in that time, with its time in ms and its sequence number, and the MODE, PADDLES and SPEED settings as the device sends them. Shows how many changes were lost.

Event lines show as they arrive, after <. The script finds the serial port by itself when there is only one; else give it with --port PORT before the steps.

A Python script can load the file and use its Device class: press, hold, shot, send, play, stop, info, get, set, stats, edges, expect, listen and drain do what the steps do. A command the device answers with ERROR raises RuntimeError.

docs.title: Every screen
docs.text:
The shots DIR step saves a screenshot of every screen into a folder: KEYER and its MEM row, the top menu list, TIMING in both views, the RECEIVE list and its five drills, the ON AIR list with POTA, SOTA, HUNT, CHEW and QUIZ, LETTERS, PROGRESS, SYSTEM, and each settings section. Start it with the device on the KEYER screen; it stops at once on any other screen. It ends there.

python3 -I tools/pocketcw.py shots shots

It keys a short QSO on KEYER, so the decode lines show only that. It keys back one group in each drill, so each shows a scored row. On POTA and SOTA it calls CQ and waits for the pileup; HUNT waits for the activator's CQ. The ragchews run until one over ends. All of them add to the practice history. KEY OUT is OFF during the run, so the tour never keys a radio, and it goes back to its value at the end. The run takes about 4 minutes. RADIO is left out, because it shows only with the decoder board on.

docs.title: The manual's screenshots
docs.text:
The manual step runs the same tour into docs/user/img, at twice the screen's size, for the pages of the user manual. It first sets the settings the screens show to their defaults, such as STYLE HAZARD, PALETTE ORANGE, SPEED 20 and TONE 700, so the images match a new device. It keeps your callsign and memories. At the end it sets each of those settings back. A setting it cannot set back shows as NOT SET BACK: NAME VALUE.

python3 -I tools/pocketcw.py manual

Each run sends new random groups and stations, so every image changes. Run it after a change to a screen, and commit the images with the change.

docs.title: Code layout
docs.text:
PocketCW is two Rust crates. Both are no_std.

Crate Path Builds for Holds pocketcw-logic logic/ Any target Keyer, decoders, drills, bots, sound synthesis, settings and records. No hardware access. pocketcw-firmware firmware/ thumbv7em-none-eabihf only Drivers, the screens, and the RTIC app in main.rs.

docs.title: Why two crates
docs.text:
Everything in logic/ runs with cargo test on your computer, with no device and no probe. The rules that decide what the device does live there: keying, decoding, scoring, the QSO and hunt bots, the battery gauge, and the byte layout of each EEPROM record. They are the parts most likely to have bugs that a test can catch.

firmware/ holds what cannot run on a computer: register access, interrupts, the screen, and the order of startup. It stays thin. It reads inputs, passes them to logic, and draws or outputs the result.

When you add code, put it in logic unless it needs a register, a pin or the screen.

docs.title: logic modules
docs.text: Module What it does keyboard USB keyboard output: the key for each decoded character, the typing queue, and the Ctrl keys for VBand. keyer The iambic and straight keyer, the key jack debounce and stuck contact rules, and the func jack output lines. decoder Decodes your own keying into characters. listen Decodes a keyed line at any speed from 5 to 60 WPM: straight key keying, and the decoder board's tone line. timing, decode_lines Grades marks and gaps, keeps keying statistics, and lays out decoded text in lines. morse, text The Morse table, prosigns, fixed size strings, and word wrap. player Sends text as Morse, with optional human timing errors. synth, volume Mixes the sidetone, up to four stations, band noise and fading into one signal. Maps volume levels to codec registers. adpcm Decodes voice clips, plays several in turn, and raises their sample rate by a whole factor. pack The content pack format: header, word list and voice clips. drill, letters, ragchew Receive drills, Koch levels, letter statistics, and ragchew QSOs. qso, hunt The bots for activating and for hunting. progress Practice history, one slot per session. memories, settings The memories and the settings, with their EEPROM records. record The EEPROM record frame and its CRC. sfdp Reads the table a serial flash chip gives about itself: size, page size, erase types and times. battery, panel, board The battery gauge, the choice of screen type and its memory read framing, and the decoder board protocol. serial Commands from the computer on the USB serial port. config Settings and memories by name, for the serial port's GET and SET. sender, winkeyer The sender that keys text from the serial port, and the WinKeyer host protocol. buttons, input, ticks, rng, math Button debounce and events, button actions, tick arithmetic, random numbers, and math helpers. dial What the dial sets on each screen, and the hold on dial turns while you key.

docs.title: firmware modules
docs.text: Module What it does main.rs The RTIC app: startup, the tasks, saving, and power off. pins Every pin number. See Pins. clock, gpio, power, fault Clock setup, pin setup, power hold and standby, and the fault screen. lcd, backlight, gfx, font, fonts, theme, boot The screen driver, drawing, fonts, styles and palettes, and the boot screen. audio, codec, es8388, wm8978 The PA8 audio output and the two audio codecs. i2c, eeprom, store The I2C bus, the EEPROM, and where each record lives. spi_flash The 16 MB SPI flash, which shares SPI1 with the screen. pack, speech Opens the content pack, and speaks text through the synth: the pack's words, and other words spelled. battery ADC readings of the battery and the supply. link The serial link to the decoder board. usb The USB device peripheral for stm32-usbd, and the USB keyboard and serial port. ui/ One file per screen, plus shared parts: dial for the header values, exchange and transcript for the QSO screens, tape for the timing tape, serial for the serial commands the screen answers. text A re-export of the fixed size string type. bin/probe.rs, bin/usbprobe.rs, bin/voiceprobe.rs, bin/flashprobe.rs, bin/popprobe.rs Separate hardware, USB, voice, SPI flash and audio pop probe images. See Build and flash.

docs.title: Tasks
docs.text:
main.rs is an RTIC 2 app. A higher priority interrupts a lower one.

Task Runs on Priority Work sample TMR1 overflow, 17,578 times a second while sound plays 4 The next audio sample. tick TMR3, every 1 ms 3 Key jack debounce, the keyer, the func jack and LED, the four players and the sidetone, both decoders, and button debounce. board_frame USART1 idle line 2 Parses a frame from the decoder board and answers it. usb_events USB interrupt, and a pend from tick 2 Answers the USB host and sends the next keyboard report. ui Async, software task 1 The boot screen, all drawing, settings changes, saves, battery polls, and power off.

tick and board_frame send messages to ui on a channel 64 messages deep. When the channel is full, a message is lost and the status line shows n INPUTS LOST.

Keying and audio never wait for the screen. A full redraw takes about 70 ms, so each event redraws only what it changed.

docs.title: Fonts
docs.text:
The screen text uses B612 Mono Regular, under the SIL Open Font License 1.1. The font file is tools/fontgen/B612Mono-Regular.ttf, and the license is firmware/src/B612-OFL.txt.

The firmware does not read the font file. tools/fontgen turns it into glyph tables in firmware/src/fonts.rs. Do not edit fonts.rs by hand: the next run of the tool replaces it.

docs.title: The two fonts
docs.text:
Font Cell Size Use SMALL 10 x 16 pixels 13 px Main text. 32 columns by 15 rows fill the 320 x 240 screen. TINY 7 x 12 pixels 10 px Labels, units and chart axes.

SMALL holds the printable ASCII characters, from space to ~. TINY holds the same set without a to z, and draws a lowercase letter as its capital. Both fonts set the baseline from all of ASCII, so they line up the same way.

docs.title: Glyph format
docs.text:
firmware/src/font.rs defines Font:

  • width, height: the cell size. Every glyph has the same cell.
  • chars: the characters, sorted by byte value. Font::draw finds a glyph by binary search.
  • boxes: per glyph, the left, top, width and height of its inked pixels inside the cell. A space has an empty box.
  • offsets: per glyph, where its pixels start in pixels, plus one entry for the end of the last glyph.
  • pixels: 4 bits of coverage per pixel, 0 to 15, high nibble first, each glyph's box row by row. Pixels outside the box are 0.

Font::draw blends from the background color to the text color by coverage. A character that is not in the font draws as a solid cell, so the gap shows on the screen.

A prosign draws as its two letters under a bar. ui/mod.rs does this in draw_char, so the fonts need no prosign glyphs.

docs.title: Make the fonts again
docs.text:
cd tools/fontgen
cargo build -r
target/release/fontgen B612Mono-Regular.ttf ../../firmware/src/fonts.rs

fontgen is its own crate, with fontdue as its only dependency. It builds for your computer.

The sizes and cells are in SPECS in tools/fontgen/src/main.rs. When a glyph has visible pixels outside its cell, the tool prints how many and writes nothing. The tool also checks that each cropped glyph unpacks to its full cell. When you change a cell size, change CHAR_W, CHAR_H, TINY_W and TINY_H in firmware/src/gfx.rs too. Asserts there stop the build when the two do not match.

The hardware probe uses the FONT_6X10 font of embedded-graphics, not these fonts.

docs.title: Release
docs.text:
A release is a git tag vX.Y.Z and a GitHub release with these files:

File Contents A000014.bin The firmware image. F000400.bin The content pack: words and voice clips for the SPI flash, installed before the firmware on a first install or when the pack changed. See Content pack. pocketcw-flash The macOS install tool, for Apple and Intel Macs. LICENSE The PocketCW license. B612-OFL.txt The license of the B612 Mono font. THIRD-PARTY.txt The MIT notice of every crate linked into the firmware, then the content pack's credits from tools/pack/pack-notice.txt.

The install script docs/install.sh downloads A000014.bin, F000400.bin and pocketcw-flash from the newest release. The docs site serves the script, so a change to it goes live when it reaches main.

docs.title: The version number
docs.text:
The version comes from version in firmware/Cargo.toml. The firmware reads it at build time, and shows it on the SYSTEM screen in the FIRMWARE row and on the boot screen.

Both crates have the same version. firmware/Cargo.toml also names the version of its pocketcw-logic dependency.

docs.title: Steps
docs.text:
Run these on a Mac. release.sh needs clang with the macOS frameworks, and the voice tools tools/pack/setup.py sets up, to build the content pack. See Content pack. With a full clip cache in firmware/target/clip-cache, the pack builds in about a minute; with only the saved speech, in about 4 minutes; with none, in about 15 minutes. cargo clean deletes the cache.

  1. Set the new version in three places: version in firmware/Cargo.toml, version in logic/Cargo.toml, and the pocketcw-logic dependency in firmware/Cargo.toml.
  2. Build once, so the Cargo.lock files take the new version. Commit everything.
  3. Build the release:
sh tools/release.sh vX.Y.Z
  1. Tag the commit and push the tag:
git tag vX.Y.Z
git push origin vX.Y.Z
  1. Make a GitHub release for the tag, and upload every file in dist/. The release notes name the release that last changed the content pack, such as "Content pack: changed in v0.4.0". Users who skip releases need this: the install script and the install page tell users to install the pack when it changed since their last install. With the GitHub CLI:
gh release create vX.Y.Z dist/*
  1. Push main last. The docs site serves install.sh from main, and the script downloads files from the newest release. So a script that needs a new release file must not go live before that release.

docs.title: What release.sh does
docs.text:
1. Stops with an error when the voice tools are not set up, when firmware/Cargo.toml does not hold the version you gave, or when the working tree has changes that are not committed. Then the files always match the tag.
  2. Runs tools/mkimage.sh and copies the image to dist/A000014.bin. Keeps the ELF in symbols/A000014-VERSION.elf for tools/panic.sh; the ELF holds local paths, so it is not uploaded.
  3. Copies LICENSE and firmware/src/B612-OFL.txt to dist/.
  4. Builds the content pack into dist/F000400.bin with tools/pack/pack.py. It prints how many common words fit.
  5. Builds dist/pocketcw-flash for Apple and Intel Macs, macOS 10.15 or later.
  6. Writes dist/THIRD-PARTY.txt with tools/notices.py and tools/pack/pack-notice.txt.
  7. Lists dist/, prints the content pack's SHA-256 for the release notes, and prints the tag and upload steps.

A pack built on another machine can differ: the clip cache key covers the Kokoro version, model and voice, and how clips are made, but not espeak-ng or FFmpeg. So the SHA-256 in the release notes records which pack shipped.

Git ignores dist/ and tools/pocketcw-flash.

docs.title: Roadmap
docs.text:
The planned work after USB: the SPI flash, copy training, two-way QSOs, and an in-line logger. Order of work:

  1. Probes: SPI flash, bootloader erase, vendor log, voice quality
  2. SPI flash driver and log location
  3. Content pack
  4. Morse then voice, and the head-copy ladder
  5. Two-way ragchew bot: deferred
  6. In-line logger: deferred until after MIDI and Vail
  7. Stats export: built
  8. More QSO kinds: P2P and S2S callers, short contest exchanges
  9. Later: send drill, keyer extras, games
  10. F key long presses: built

docs.title: Ground facts
docs.text:
• Storage, and what each holds:
Store Size Free Holds MCU flash 241,664 bytes 72.2 KiB at opt-level = "z" (image 167,772 bytes on 2026-10-27) Code, and small tables the core features need without a pack. Code cannot run from the SPI flash: it sits on SPI1, not a memory-mapped interface. SPI flash (F files) 16 MB About 13 MB outside the vendor regions Content pack, voice packs, log. EEPROM (I2C) 2 KB 64 bytes (0x7C0 to 0x7FF) Settings, letter stats, progress, memories. Too small for the log; the plan only appends the LOG setting to the settings record. RAM 64 KB About 56 KB Buffers, such as the 16 KB voice clip buffer.
  • opt-level = "z" is adopted: the app ran fine on hardware. The sample interrupt costs 1092 of 4096 cycles for one sine voice, and at most 1812 with square waves, noise and fading, at "z" on board 2.64 (INFO AUDIO, 2026-10-27).
  • USB MIDI is planned next, and will take MCU flash.
  • SPI flash: 16 MB GigaDevice GD25Q128 (JEDEC C8 40 18), on SPI1 with the LCD (LCD_CS PB6, FLASH_CS PB9). No write protection is set. SFDP 1.0 with 9 dwords lists 4 KB (0x20), 32 KB (0x52) and 64 KB (0xD8) erase, but no erase times and no page size.
  • SPI flash in use, by scan: 0x000000 to 0x025FFF (boot screen), 0x030000 to 0x0C5FFF (UI images), 0x100000 to about 0x8FC000 (the content pack F000400.bin), 0xE00000 to 0xFECFFF (fonts). Free: 0x0C6000 to 0x0FFFFF and 0x8FC000 to 0xDFFFFF. The stock firmware has a contact log whose location is not known, so a pack install may erase it.
  • Install limit: pocketcw-flash refuses a file that needs more than one FAT sector (tools/pocketcw-flash.c:250): 1022 clusters. The update drive has 8 KB clusters, so 8,372,224 bytes. An 8.37 MB install is tested.
  • An install erases and writes only the 4 KB sectors its file covers. Data in the next sector is kept.
  • No RTC (PC14 and PC15 carry the dial) and no audio input (no I2S lines to the MCU).
  • Task model: sample at priority 4, tick at 3, ui at 1. The audio resource is shared by tick and ui, so its lock masks the 1 ms tick. The event queue to ui is 64 deep.
  • The serial port is in main: text commands, WinKeyer mode and the VBand CW Hotline (docs/dev/serial.md). The port is up while USB OUT is anything but OFF; USB OUT SERIAL gives the port alone, with no typing.
  • Logic goes in logic/ with host tests; firmware/ stays thin. See Code layout.

docs.title: 1. Probes
docs.text: All four go in probe images. None needs the flash driver in the main image. Each has a pass rule that can fail.

docs.title: SPI flash
docs.text:
• JEDEC ID (0x9F), status registers 1 to 3 (0x05, 0x35, 0x15), SFDP (0x5A). Take erase sizes and timings from SFDP, not from a part name, since clone parts are common.
  • Pass: SFDP reads, 4 KB sector erase is listed, and no protect bit (BP, TB, SEC, CMP, SRP) covers the free area.
  • Read 0x100000 and compare it with F000400.bin, at 18 MHz and at 4.5 MHz. Pass: both match.
  • Erase and program one 4 KB sector in the free area and read it back, timing the erase. Pass: the data matches, and the worst erase time is recorded.
  • Program 16 partial writes into one 256 byte page, then read it back. The log appends small records into pages, and some parts limit partial programs per page. Pass: all 16 match.

Passed on 2026-10-25. Erase takes 15 ms on a blank sector and 45 ms on a programmed one; a page programs in at most 917 µs. See Storage.

docs.title: Bootloader erase
docs.text:
Done on 2026-10-25 with firmware/src/bin/flashprobe.rs and tools/flashtest.py. See SPI flash probe.

  • The update drive has 8 KB clusters and 51,200 sectors of 2 KB. pocketcw-flash prints both.
  • A 2,093,056 byte test file at 0x100000 installed in full: 511 tagged sectors, 0x100000 to 0x2FEFFF.
  • Markers at the file's end, plus 4 KB, plus 64 KB, plus 1 MB, and at 0xC00000 and 0xDFF000 all survived.
  • Result: an install touches only the sectors its file covers. The log range is safe.

docs.title: Vendor log
docs.text:
• On a unit that has run stock firmware, scan 0x0C5080 to 0xDFFFFF for bytes that are not 0xFF. That shows where the vendor contact log lives, so the PocketCW log does not overlap it and a return to stock does not wipe it.
  • Deferred until a Pro unit is available. The 2.64 unit has no stock contact log, and its free area reads blank.

docs.title: Voice quality
docs.text:
Done on 2026-10-25 with firmware/src/bin/voiceprobe.rs. See Voice probe.

  • Three candidate voices: Kokoro-82M af_heart, Piper LJSpeech, and espeak-ng, one probe image each. Each plays 20 words at 8789 Hz and 20 at 5859 Hz.
  • Kokoro was clear. Piper had a better tone but cut off word endings ("egg" sounded like "ek"). espeak-ng sounded least human.
  • On the speaker, 8789 Hz and 5859 Hz sounded the same. Headphones are not checked yet.
  • Result: Kokoro af_heart at 5859 Hz.
  • Then, with the content pack on the speaker, 5859 Hz lost the ends of letters: QTH sounded like QT8. A listening pack (tools/pack/listenpack.py) compared 5859, 8789 and 17,578 Hz. 8789 Hz with a treble boost was clear, and 17,578 Hz best. The pack moved to 8789 Hz for every clip, since one rate for letters and another for words would be jarring. The same tests found foreign vowels from the phoneme form, and rushed lone letters; see Content pack.

docs.title: 2. SPI flash driver and log location
Bus sharing
docs.text: Lcd owns pac::SPI1 today. Split it into a Bus that owns SPI1 and both chip selects, with Lcd and Flash as users. All flash access runs in the ui task, which already owns every LCD draw, so no lock is needed. read_row changes the SPI divider and the MISO mode (lcd.rs), so the flash driver sets both on every transaction.

docs.title: Erase without blocking
docs.text:
• Only 4 KB sector erase. No block or chip erase.
  • The bus is free while the chip erases. The driver starts an erase and returns. Every later command but a status read first waits while the chip is busy, so other ui work keeps running, and a content pack read during an erase waits for it. Built.
  • The log erases its next sector ahead, when the head sector is half full and the key is idle. A record write is then only page programs of a few ms.

docs.title: Layout
docs.text:
Only the log is persisted user data, so only its location is fixed now: 0xC00000 to 0xDFFFFF (2 MB), the top of the free area. 0xBF0000 to 0xBFFFFF is a guard that nothing writes. The step 1 probes showed the range blank and untouched by installs.

The packs grow up from 0x100000 and end below the guard. Installs rewrite them and they ship with matching firmware, so each release can move or resize them. Each pack file is 8,372,224 bytes or less, at a 64 KB aligned offset (F000400.bin at 0x100000, F000C00.bin at 0x300000, and so on).

The logic crate holds the layout and an allowed(address, len) check (logic/src/log.rs). The driver refuses any erase or program outside the log range. Host tests cover the check. Built.

Flash cost: about 3 KB.

docs.title: 3. Content pack
docs.text:
F000400.bin, built by a Python tool from text in the repo. Format 4 of the existing header (PocketCW, format byte):

  • Header: magic, format version, a table of sections (kind, offset, length, CRC32).
  • Sections are added as the features that use them arrive: word lists by frequency first, for the head-copy ladder.

The device parses the header in logic, with host tests on packs the tool builds. Features that need a missing section show CONTENT PACK MISSING: INSTALL IT; the rest of the firmware works.

The core bots must work without a pack. Their tables stay in MCU flash unless the flash budget forces a move; then a small fallback table stays.

Flash cost: about 1 KB.

docs.title: 4. Morse then voice, and the head-copy ladder
What it does
docs.text:
• NINJA drill: the device sends a word in Morse, waits, then speaks it. No keying needed. Key the word before the voice, and it is scored like the other drills. Built as a fourth receive drill, with single words from the content pack; phrases are not built.
  • Head-copy ladder: words get longer as you copy them, then two words, then short sentences. You key back at the end. Built as a fifth receive drill, HEAD, with QSO exchange lines as the sentences.
  • HEAD keeps its rung across power off, in the settings record.
  • Maybe for HEAD: the voice says the item after your copy, as in NINJA. The pack would first need clips for every word of the QSO lines (names, cities, rigs, weather), which is a pack change.

docs.title: Voice clips
docs.text:
• Voice: Kokoro-82M af_heart, built on a computer with tools/pack/voiceclips.py. The probe picked it among three, each with a license that allows redistribution of its output:
Voice License Kokoro-82M Apache 2.0 weights, trained on permissive or public domain audio. The CC BY data in it covers Japanese and French voices; af_heart is American English. Piper LJSpeech Public domain dataset. Other Piper voices carry their own licenses and are not candidates. espeak-ng GPL-3.0. Robotic, but formant speech can stay clear at low sample rates.
  • tools/release.sh appends the content pack's credits, tools/pack/pack-notice.txt, to THIRD-PARTY.txt.
  • Format: 4-bit IMA ADPCM at 8789 Hz (17578 / 2), about 4.4 KB a second. Playback draws two output samples per input on straight lines (logic/src/adpcm.rs), so no fractional resampler is needed. The pack header gives the rate, so a pack at another rate needs no firmware change.
  • Size: a pack file is 8,372,224 bytes or less, about 1900 s of speech. tools/pack/pack.py leaves out the least common words until the pack fits. An 8.37 MB pack installed and played its first and last clips.
  • Built: tools/pack/audition.py plays every clip as the device plays it, so a listener can mark the bad ones without the device and fix them with a respelling or phonemes. Marks and fixes are kept per voice, in tools/pack/voices. See Reviewing the clips.

docs.title: Playback
docs.text:
• The ui task reads a whole clip into a ui-owned 16 KB buffer, outside every lock. 16 KB holds about 3.7 s at 8789 Hz. The clip builder fails any clip, or any word or spelling and meaning together, longer than the buffer, so the limit is checked at build time.
  • It hands the buffer to the sample task through a single-producer, single-consumer index: no copy under the audio lock.
  • The sample task decodes ADPCM and plays it as one more voice in synth. The cost is tens of cycles a sample against 4096 available.
  • Built: SAY on the serial port speaks text. Words with a clip in the pack play it; other words, and words the pack spells such as QTH, are spelled from character clips (tools/pack/words/chars.txt), up to 32 clips in the 16 KB buffer. One abbreviation on its own also gets its meaning, 200 ms after the word. Clips play in turn with 120 ms between them.

Flash cost: about 4 KB.

docs.title: 5. Two-way ragchew bot
docs.text: Deferred on 2026-10-25. The POTA and SOTA modes already give two-way practice, and its 6 to 10 KB of flash goes to Vail and MIDI support instead.

docs.title: What it does
docs.text: You are one of the two stations. The bot calls CQ or answers yours. The QSO runs as on the air: reports, names, QTH, rig, antenna, weather, then 73. The bot answers what you send: it sends your report back, uses your name, asks AGN? about a field it could not read, and answers QRS and ?.

docs.title: Design
docs.text:
• A new logic/src/chat.rs, next to ragchew.rs (which keeps the listen-only kinds), built on its Station data. Answers longer than 48 characters split into lines as ragchew.rs already does.
  • Your overs are longer than the current buffer: the over buffer is 48 characters and the parsers take 16 words. Chat needs its own over buffer of about 300 characters.
  • Over end: ragchew senders pause mid-over, so three word gaps (decoder.rs COPY_END_UNITS) would cut them off. Chat ends an over on K, KN, <BK>, <AR> or <SK> after DE <call>, and on a long silence as fallback.
  • Parser: your name and QTH are unknown values, so tolerance applies to the keywords (NAME, OP, QTH, UR, RST, RIG, ANT, WX) and to the bot's own fields. The token after a keyword is taken as given. When a doubled token disagrees (BOB BOP), the bot asks AGN?.
  • Scoring: copy is scored with the existing Ragchew::question after the QSO, so you send what you would on the air. Scores go to Letters and Progress.

docs.title: Tests
docs.text:
Host tests run scripted QSOs: a clean one, one with an error in each field, one with AGN, QRS and ?, and one with mid-over pauses. On hardware, the serial SEND command keys a whole QSO.

Flash cost: 6 to 10 KB, the largest item.

docs.title: 6. In-line logger
docs.text:
Deferred on 2026-10-25, after MIDI and Vail. F key holds are built, so note mode can take a hold outside the menu. Built and kept: the log ring and format (logic/src/log.rs), and the flash write guard (firmware/src/spi_flash.rs). Built and taken out: run capture, the LOG setting, DUMP LOG and pocketcw.py log, in commit d920c55; commit 3bb0d26 takes them out, and a revert of 3bb0d26 puts them back.

Open questions for when it returns:

  • Note mode and the LOG screen need a place. LOG fits in STATS. Note mode fits on a hold; the F1 hold is the user's one shortcut, and the menu lists hold 7 rows without scrolling, so a new row needs menu scrolling first.
  • A run ends after 4 s with no new text. Check this against real sending.
  • A memory is logged whole at the end of its playback, and only from STRAIGHT output with KEY OUT on.
  • On a Pro, check whether the decoder board hears your own sidetone. If it does, your keying logs twice, as YOU and as THEM.
  • A memory's run ends when the "playback ended" message arrives. A full event queue can drop that message, and the run then stays open until the next memory or power off.

The device sits between your key and the radio with KEY OUT on, and records a raw transcript. The device does no QSO detection. tools/pocketcw.py finds QSOs in the exported transcript.

docs.title: Why detection runs on the computer
docs.text:
• Python has no flash budget, no 48 character buffers, and full regex and fuzzy matching.
  • A better rule re-reads every transcript ever recorded, with no firmware release.
  • Real exported transcripts are the test files, and a test run takes seconds.
  • On-device QSO records can come later as a new record kind. The log walker skips kinds it does not know, so that is an addition, not a migration.

What the device loses: a live contact count in the field ("do I have my 10?"). Accepted for now. A later on-device count is an addition.

docs.title: Turning it on
docs.text:
• LOG in the DEVICE section: ON or OFF, default OFF. Bit 4 of the settings record's hardware flags byte, which older firmware ignores, so the record length stays the same.
  • While LOG is ON with the decoder board on, the decoder board listener also runs (Pro only). Today it runs only on the RADIO screen or with USB OUT RADIO.

docs.title: What goes in the transcript
docs.text:
• YOU: what the decoder reads from your keying.
  • MEMORY: the text of each memory that keys the radio. Memory playback does not pass through the decoder, so the text is logged directly.
  • NOTE: text keyed in note mode. The key writes to the log and KEY OUT stays off. A hunter on a Mini never sends the activator's call, so a note is the only way it reaches the log. Note mode shows on the screen while it is on, and ends after one note, so it cannot silently stop transmitting. Note mode starts from a hold on KEYER, such as F2 or F3, which have none yet.
  • THEM (Pro only): the decoder board text. The Pro is untested.

Text is buffered in RAM and written once per over or note, not once per character. Power off, including the battery-empty path, writes the buffers first.

docs.title: Time
docs.text: No clock and no time entry. A session is one power-on. Times are milliseconds since boot (u32, 49 days). pocketcw.py takes an optional start time per session to fill QSO_DATE and TIME_ON in ADIF. POTA upload needs them.

docs.title: Log format
docs.text:
Persisted, so decided now.

Ring:

  • One ring in the log range, as a run of 4 KB sectors. A record never crosses a sector.
  • Every sector starts with a header record, written when the sector is first used. A sector with no valid header is erased again before use, since a torn erase can read as 0xFF and still be weak. A sector erased ahead and not yet used has no header, so after a power-off it is erased again; that costs one erase.
  • The sector header stays version 1 forever, and its fields only append. Older firmware erases a sector whose header it cannot read, so a new header version would wipe the log on a downgrade.

Records use the logic/src/record.rs frame: magic (2 bytes), version, body length (1 byte), body, CRC16. The magic is L and a kind letter, so its first byte is never 0xFF.

Kind Magic Body, version 1 Sector header LH sequence u32, session u32 (the session open when the sector started) Session start LS session u32, start tick u32, firmware version (major, minor, patch: 3 bytes), callsign length u8, callsign (up to 10) Transcript run LT source u8 (YOU 0, MEMORY 1, NOTE 2, THEM 3), run id u16 (counted per session), part u8 (bit 7 set: more parts follow), start tick u32, end tick u32, text length u8, text (up to 242)

Numbers are little-endian. Text is ASCII as the screen shows it: a prosign as its letters in angle brackets (<AR>), an unknown character as *, a word gap as one space.

Runs and parts:

  • A run is one over or note of one source. It ends after 4 s with no new text from that source.
  • A run longer than 242 characters goes in parts. A part is written with bit 7 set only once the next character arrives, so the bit never promises a part that does not come. A reader still accepts a last part with bit 7 set, since power loss can cut a run.
  • Parts join by plain concatenation. Each part's start and end ticks give that part's own span. A run ends at part 127, and the next character starts a new run.
  • The session start record is written before the first run of a power-on, so a power-on with nothing logged writes nothing. Its start tick is the time it was written.

Fixed fields come first and text last, behind its own length, so later versions can append fields after the text. The session-start record carries your callsign for ADIF STATION_CALLSIGN, since it can change between sessions. Start and end ticks order YOU and THEM runs that overlap.

Walking a sector:

  • First byte 0xFF: end of data.
  • A known kind whose body is too short for its fields or text length: skipped.
  • Length past the sector, or a bad CRC: torn. The sector is closed and writing goes on in the next one.
  • Valid frame of an unknown kind or version: skipped. record::unframe cannot be used here, since it rejects every other magic and version as if corrupt.

Startup:

  • The head is the sector with the highest sequence. The next session number is one more than the highest session in the head sector.
  • With no valid header anywhere (the first boot), the first write goes to the first sector, with sequence 1 and session 1.
  • A torn record in the head closes it, so the next write goes to the next sector.
  • The session counter lives in the log, not in the EEPROM boot count, which does not advance when its write fails.

Wrap:

  • When the ring wraps, the oldest sector goes. A 2 MB ring holds hundreds of activations.
  • The oldest surviving sector can start mid-session and mid-run. Its header gives the session. A reader drops the parts of a run whose part 0 is gone.

docs.title: On the device
docs.text:
• DUMP LOG on the serial port sends the raw records. Set USB OUT to SERIAL to export.
  • LOG screen: a transcript viewer. Scroll back through past sessions by session number, with each run marked by its source.

docs.title: On the computer
docs.text:
• pocketcw.py log reads the dump and writes a text transcript per session.
  • pocketcw.py adif proposes QSOs from the transcript and writes ADIF. Activating: your <call> 5NN, then TU <state> 72. Hunting: your call sent to an activator, then a NOTE with its call. QSOs it is not sure of are marked for you to check.

docs.title: Tests
docs.text:
• Device, on host: wrap, torn record, torn erase, a future-kind record between two known ones (both known records read), a wrap where the oldest sector begins with part 2 of a run, session start replay, next session number at startup.
  • Device, on hardware: power off during a write, then check the log reads back. Battery-empty power off flushes the buffers.
  • Computer: QSO detection runs only after you record real activations. Those transcripts, with the QSOs you logged by hand, are the test fixtures.

Flash cost: 4 to 5 KB (ring, DUMP LOG, note mode, LOG screen).

docs.title: 7. Stats export
docs.text:
Built: STATS LETTERS, STATS PROGRESS and STATS TIMING on the serial port, and pocketcw.py stats saves each as CSV. See Stats. Timing statistics are not saved across power off, and the EEPROM has 64 bytes left, so a saved version would go in the log as a new kind.

Flash cost: 4.0 KB, measured.

docs.title: P2P and S2S callers
docs.text:
Park to park (P2P) and summit to summit (S2S) contacts are common. Today only Hunt takes a P2P call from you, and no bot sends a reference.

  • Activate: some hunters are at a park or on a summit. Such a hunter sends P2P or S2S and its reference in the exchange, such as RR TU 559 CA CA P2P US-1234 72 or S2S W7O/CN-001. Confirm the current POTA reference format before building: POTA moved from K-1234 to country codes such as US-1234.
  • Hunt: from a park or summit you send P2P or S2S and your reference; the activator answers with its own.
  • Copy check: the contact counts as copied when your closing holds the other station's reference.
  • Tables: a few dozen park and summit references per call area, chosen to match the hunter's state.

Flash cost: 1 to 2 KB.

docs.title: Short contest exchanges
docs.text:
Contests are short, fixed exchanges at speed: no 72 or 73, often only TU and your call to close. Add them as programs in Activate, beside POTA and SOTA: you call CQ TEST, the bot sends a pileup, and each caller sends one exchange.

Contest Exchange Example CWT Name and member number, or state for a non-member BOB 1234, BOB TX SST Name and state BOB TX SKCC sprint RST, state, name and member number 579 TX BOB 12345T Field Day Class and ARRL section 2A STX
  • Copy check: you key the exchange you copied, as Hunt logs a callsign. Each field scores apart.
  • Names and states come from the ragchew and hunter tables. New tables: member numbers (made at random), Field Day classes and ARRL sections.

Flash cost: 2 to 3 KB.

docs.title: Flash budget
docs.text:
Item Estimate SPI flash driver 3 KB Content pack parser 1 KB Voice and head copy 4 KB Two-way ragchew (deferred) 6 to 10 KB Logger, LOG screen, DUMP LOG (deferred) 4 to 5 KB; capture and DUMP LOG measured 5.6 KB Stats export 4.0 KB, measured P2P and S2S callers 1 to 2 KB Short contest exchanges 2 to 3 KB Total, without the deferred items 15 to 17 KB

The plan needs 15 to 17 KB of 72.2 KiB free at "z", before MIDI. The cleanup on 2026-10-27 took back 54,368 bytes: panic messages, float formatting, a copy of the Text write code per size, full font cells, the Two-Way string search, core's sort and a 64-bit divide. More ways to get flash back:

  • Move fixed text tables (ragchew names, cities, rigs; bot phrases) into the content pack, with a small fallback in MCU flash so the bots still work without a pack.
  • Look at the largest symbols (llvm-nm --size-sort) for the next large item.

If flash stays short, set a budget per feature: which features ship first.

docs.title: Revisit at the end
docs.text:
1. F key long presses: built. A hold is a second action per F key, so controls like note mode need not live in a menu.
  2. When the serial port is up: today only while USB OUT is not OFF. Option: up whenever USB is plugged in, with USB OUT choosing only what types.

docs.title: Serial interface
docs.text: PocketCW has a USB serial port that a computer uses to press the buttons, key and play text, read what the device decodes and plays, read and change the settings, read the stats and the key timing, and read the screen. Remote control and screenshots covers the harness that uses it.

docs.title: The port
docs.text:
The device is a composite USB device: a keyboard and a CDC-ACM serial port, with Artery's composite example ID, 2E3C:5750. It is on USB while USB OUT is anything but OFF. SERIAL gives the port alone, with no typing. With USB OUT set to OFF, the device detaches and the port goes away.

The port shows up as /dev/cu.usbmodem* on macOS and /dev/ttyACM* on Linux. The device ignores the baud rate and the other line settings.

The port has two modes. It starts in text mode, which the sections below up to WinKeyer describe. A 0x00 byte switches it to WinKeyer mode.

docs.title: Commands
docs.text:
Each command is one line of up to 55 bytes, ended by \n or \r. Commands are upper case, except the two that VBand sends; text and values may be lower case. The device skips empty lines, answers a line it does not know with ERROR UNKNOWN, and answers a longer line, or text over 48 characters, with ERROR TOO LONG.

Command Device PRESS F1 to PRESS F4 Presses and releases that soft key. No reply. HOLD F1 to HOLD F4 Presses that soft key, holds it past its hold time, and releases it. No reply. The dial cannot be held, since a held click turns the device off. PRESS LEFT, PRESS RIGHT Turns the dial one step. No reply. PRESS CLICK Presses and releases the dial. No reply. SEND TEXT Keys up to 48 characters of text. See Send. PLAY TEXT Sounds up to 48 characters of text. See Play. SAY TEXT Speaks up to 48 characters from the content pack: each word the pack has a clip for, and every other word, such as QTH, spelled a character at a time. One abbreviation on its own also gets its meaning: SAY QTH says "Q T H. location", and SAY QTH IS says "Q T H is". Answers OK SAY TEXT, or ERROR SAY: NO PACK, or ERROR SAY: NOTHING TO SAY. Speech stops at about 3.7 s or 32 clips. A screen change, or a drill's STOP, also stops it. Lower case counts as upper case; a prosign is written as <BK>. STOP Stops the text of SEND and PLAY, and anything else the device is sounding. No reply. SHOT Sends the screen. See Screenshot. INFO Answers INFO VERSION=0.2.0 SCREEN=KEYER PANEL=IPS PACK=3131 AUDIO=1900/4096: the firmware version, the screen, the panel (IPS or ILI9341), the content pack's word count, or NONE, OLD for a pack of an earlier format, or BAD for a corrupt one, and the sample interrupt's longest run since the last INFO against its budget, in CPU cycles. GET NAME, GET Sends a setting or memory, or all of them. See Settings. SET NAME VALUE Changes a setting or memory. See Settings. EDGE ON, EDGE OFF Starts or stops the key timing lines. See Edges. VBand On, VBand Off Starts or stops the CW Hotline lines, in this mixed case. See VBand Hotline. No reply. STATS LETTERS, STATS PROGRESS, STATS TIMING Sends the letter stats, the practice sessions, or your keying timing. See Stats.

Every command goes to the screen through one queue, in the order it came, so a screenshot after a press shows the result of the press. A press skips the debounce, so it cannot hold a button: PRESS CLICK does not power off. More than about 30 commands sent at once can fill the queue; the device then shows n INPUTS LOST.

The screen waits for room in the serial queue for each reply line, for up to 0.5 s; a line that waits longer is lost, with the rest of its reply, and counts in n SERIAL LINES LOST. Event lines can come between the lines of a reply.

docs.title: Send
docs.text:
SEND keys its text as a straight key with perfect timing, at the keyer speed. Lower case counts as upper case, and a prosign is written in angle brackets, such as <AR>. A character with no Morse code is skipped.

The keying takes the same path as the paddle: the decoder, the screen, the sidetone and the LED. Every screen sees it as your keying, so it answers drills and works QSOs. KEY OUT keys the radio when it is ON and OUT TYPE is STRAIGHT. Touching the key or sending a memory stops the text. The text stops a memory that is sending or waiting to repeat.

One word gap after the text ends, the device sends SENT. By then the decoder has sent the last character and the word gap as KEY lines. A SEND before the SENT of the one before gets BUSY and is not keyed.

docs.title: Play
docs.text: PLAY sounds its text as the receive drills do: at CHAR SPEED and FARNSWORTH, on TONE, with NOISE and FADING on every screen while it sounds. Lower case counts as upper case, and a prosign is written in angle brackets. It does not key the radio, and the decoder does not hear it. The PLAY event line comes when it starts, and PLAYED when everything the device is sounding has finished. A PLAY while a drill sounds plays beside it on a free voice.

docs.title: Settings
docs.text:
A name is a settings row with _ for each space: MODE, PADDLES, SPEED, KEY_OUT, OUT_TYPE, OUT_LINES, USB_OUT, TONE, VOLUME, WAVE, NOISE, FADING, CHAR_SPEED, FARNSWORTH, CHEW_SHOWS, NINJA_WORDS, DECODER_BOARD, PILEUP, FIST, SPEED_SPREAD, STYLE, PALETTE, BRIGHTNESS and F1_HOLD. A value is what the row shows, without WPM, HZ or %: IAMBIC B, ON, 25, MATCH.

The memories have their own names:

Name Value CALL Your callsign: up to 10 of A to Z, 0 to 9 and /. M1 to M4 A memory's text, up to 48 characters, with a prosign written as <AR>. Repeated spaces drop out. MEM_EVERY Seconds between repeats of a held memory, 2 to 30. MEM_STAY_OPEN ON or OFF. Command Reply GET SPEED VALUE SPEED 25 GET A VALUE line for every name, then END. SET SPEED 25 OK SPEED 25. The device redraws the screen and saves the change as it does from the dial. SET SPEED 70 ERROR SPEED: 5 TO 60. Nothing changes. The reason lists the values the setting takes.

SET cannot turn USB off: SET USB_OUT OFF, and SET DECODER_BOARD OFF while USB OUT is RADIO, answer an error. Set them on the device.

docs.title: Edges
docs.text:
After EDGE ON, the device sends a line for each change on the key and paddle lines, until EDGE OFF or the computer closes the port:

EDGE KEY 1 123456 4021

The line is KEY for the keyed signal, from the paddles or a SEND, and TIP and RING for the paddle contacts. 1 is closed or down and 0 open or up. The third field is the time on the device's millisecond count.

The last field is the sequence number. The device counts every change on these lines, sent or not, and the count wraps after 2^32 - 1 to 0. A jump of more than one between two lines means lines were lost between them: in a full queue to the screen, or in a full serial queue, which counts in n SERIAL LINES LOST.

EDGE ON answers with the settings a replay of the lines needs, and the device sends them again whenever one changes while edge lines are on:

VALUE MODE IAMBIC B
VALUE PADDLES NORMAL
VALUE SPEED 25

docs.title: VBand Hotline
docs.text:
VBand's page can read keying from a serial port, as it does from a CW Hotline. It opens the port at 115200 baud and writes VBand On; when its Disconnect button is clicked, it writes VBand Off. In between, the device sends one line for each mark of the signal that keys the radio: your keying, SEND text and memories.

SM,3000,60
SM,60,180

The first field is the space before the mark and the second is the mark, both in ms and at most 3000. The first mark after VBand On, and any mark after a longer space, has a space of 3000, which VBand plays as the start of an over. A line comes when its mark ends. VBand skips every other line, so the event lines can go on beside these.

While the Hotline is on, the device sends no keyboard reports. It ends on VBand Off, or when the computer closes the port.

docs.title: Stats
docs.text:
STATS LETTERS sends LEVEL n, the number of Koch characters in play, then one line for each Koch character in Koch order, then the mixups, most common first, then END:

LETTER K 15 80 KNOWN
MIXUP A N 3

A LETTER line gives the character, its tries, the percent copied right, and KNOWN, UNSURE, WEAK, or NEW for a character not yet sent. A MIXUP line gives the character sent, the one copied, and how often.

STATS PROGRESS sends one line for each practice session, oldest first, then END:

SESSION 12 600 3 120 100 450

The fields are the session number, the seconds of practice, the contacts logged, the characters sent in receive drills, how many of those you copied right, and the characters you keyed.

STATS TIMING sends the timing of your keying since power on, or since you last cleared the TIMING screen, then END:

MARK DIT 120 62.40 4.10
MARK DAH 118 190.25 9.80
GAP ELEMENT 210 1.02 0.15
GAP CHAR 40 3.10 0.42
GAP WORD 9 7.80 1.25
RATIO 3.05
WPM 19.60
BINS MARK 4 0 0 0 1 12 ...
BINS GAP 8 0 2 ...
RELEASE 40 1.12 0.45
CLOSE 3
LATE 5 0.21 0.10
ON_TIME 95
TIP DIT 0 - -
TIP DAH 0 - -
RING DIT 0 - -
RING DAH 0 - -
WEIGHT 0 - -
OVERLAP 0
BINS RELEASE 3 0 3 2 5 ...
  • A MARK or GAP line gives the count, the mean and the standard deviation. Marks are in ms; gaps are in dots of the keyer speed at the time. The standard deviation divides by the count, so one sample gives 0. - stands for a value that needs at least one sample.
  • RATIO is the dah length over the dit length; 3 is standard. WPM is the speed your timing works out to. Each line comes only once its value is known.
  • A BINS line is a histogram: the range in dots, then the count in each of its equal bins from 0: 24 for MARK and GAP, 12 for RELEASE. The last bin also holds everything longer than the range.
  • The lines from RELEASE on measure the paddle or key contacts. See Timing. RELEASE is the time from your last release to the keyer's decision at the end of each iambic character, in dots. CLOSE counts the releases under half a dot. LATE is how far past the decision you pressed, in dots, for each gap inside a character you started late; ON_TIME counts the others. TIP and RING are the dots and dashes in ms each contact keyed in STRAIGHT mode, and WEIGHT is each such dot over the gap after it. OVERLAP counts those marks during which the other contact closed too.
  • Numbers have two decimals.
  • Marks in ms mix speeds when SPEED changes after a clear. Text that SEND keys counts in the MARK and GAP lines, since it keys the same line, but has no contacts for the lines after them.

docs.title: Events
docs.text:
While the computer has the port open (holds DTR), the device sends a line for each of these:

Line When KEY C The decoder read character C from your keying. A word gap is KEY and one space; a pattern with no character is KEY *; a prosign is KEY <AR>. HEARD C The decoder board's tone line gave character C, written as for KEY. PLAY TEXT The device started to sound TEXT: a drill group, a station's line, or a memory. PLAYED Everything the device was sounding has finished. SENT The text of a SEND has finished. BUSY A SEND came before the last one finished. EDGE LINE 1 MS SEQ A key or paddle line changed, after EDGE ON. See Edges. VALUE NAME VALUE After EDGE ON, a keyer setting at the start and when it changes. See Edges. SM,SPACE,MARK A mark ended, after VBand On. See VBand Hotline.

PLAY gives a drill group before you hear it, so a script can answer it. Event lines never break into a screenshot: the screen sends them in turn with its other work. An event line that finds the serial queue full is lost, and the screen shows n SERIAL LINES LOST.

docs.title: Screenshot
docs.text:
The device answers SHOT with a header line, then the screen:

SHOT 320 240 RGB666\n

After the header come 240 rows, top to bottom, each 320 pixels left to right: 230400 bytes. Each pixel is 3 bytes, red, green, blue, with the channel in the top 6 bits of its byte. To make an 8-bit channel from byte b, copy the top bits down: b & 0xFC | b >> 6.

The bytes are the panel's memory, read back over SPI with RAMRD. See Memory read. The screen stops for under a second while a screenshot sends.

Answer or status Cause SHOT UNCHECKED PANEL and a line end, in place of the header The board has the ILI9341 panel, whose memory read is not checked. No rows follow. SCREENSHOT NOT SENT on the screen USB took nothing for 0.5 s, so the device stopped sending.

A screenshot that stops early can leave its bytes queued. The device drops them only when USB detaches, so closing the port keeps them. A reader looks for SHOT to find the next header.

docs.title: WinKeyer
docs.text:
The device answers the K1EL WinKeyer host protocol as a WK2 with firmware 23, so logging programs can key through it. K1EL's WinKeyer 3 datasheet (rev 1.3) defines the protocol; this section lists what the device does with it.

No text command starts with 0x00, so a 0x00 byte starts the WinKeyer parser. Until host open, the parser takes only admin commands (00 nn). Host open (00 02) answers 23 and starts WinKeyer mode. Host close (00 03), reset (00 01), the computer dropping DTR, and USB detaching all end it: the queued text is dropped, the port goes back to text mode, and event lines start again. Text mode sends no event lines while WinKeyer mode is on.

Text bytes go to the same sender as SEND, which keys them in the same path. A queue holds 128 characters and buffered commands. Upper case letters, digits and the signs in morse key as themselves. The WinKeyer prosign signs key as merged pairs, such as < for AR and = for BT. | is half a dot of silence. Lower case and other bytes above ] are ignored, as on a WinKeyer.

Command Device 00 04 nn echo test Sends back nn. 00 05, 00 06, 00 07, 00 15, 00 18 Sends back 0. 00 09 firmware major revision Sends back 23. 00 0A set WK1 mode Stops the pushbutton bytes. 00 0B set WK2 mode Starts the pushbutton bytes. 00 17 firmware minor revision Sends back 0. 02 nn speed Sets SPEED to nn WPM, clamped to 5 to 60, and saves it; 0 keeps it. 05 min range x speed pot setup Sets the lowest speed of the pot reply. 06 nn pause Holds the queue while nn is not 0. 07 get speed pot Sends back 0x80 plus SPEED less the pot's lowest speed, at most 31. 08 backspace Drops the newest queued item. 0A clear buffer Stops and drops the queue. 0B nn key immediate Holds the key down while nn is not 0. 0E nn WinKeyer mode Bit 2 turns serial echo on, bit 6 paddle echo. The other bits are ignored. 0F load defaults (15 values) Takes the mode, the speed and the pot's lowest speed. 15 request status Sends back the status byte. 1B a b merge letters Keys a and b as one character. 1C nn buffered speed Keys the queued items after it at nn WPM. 1E cancel buffered speed Goes back to SPEED.

The device reads the parameter bytes of every other command and ignores them, so the bytes after them keep their meaning. 00 0D load EEPROM skips its 256 bytes; 00 0C dump EEPROM sends nothing back.

docs.title: Bytes to the host
docs.text:
Byte When Status, 0xC0 with flags On request, and on each change. Bit 2 BUSY: the queue is keying or holds text. Bit 1 BREAKIN: the paddles keyed within a word gap. Bit 0 XOFF: the queue is over 2/3 full. Speed pot, 0x80 plus SPEED less the pot's lowest speed On request, and when SPEED changes on the device. A speed the host set sends none. Pushbutton, 0xC8 with a bit for the button down In WK2 mode, when F1 to F4 go down and up: bit 0 for F1, 1 for F2, 2 for F3, 4 for F4. The screen does not see them then. Serial echo Each text byte, once its last mark ends, while serial echo is on. A prosign sign such as < echoes itself; a 1B merge echoes nothing. Paddle echo Each character the decoder reads from the paddles, and a space for a word gap, while paddle echo is on. A prosign with a WinKeyer sign echoes the sign, such as + for AR; one with no sign echoes nothing.

A byte that finds the queue to the host full is lost, and the screen shows n WINKEYER BYTES LOST. So is a text byte that finds the key queue full.

The text keys with perfect timing, at the WinKeyer speed. The paddles keep the device's MODE and PADDLES, and the sidetone keeps TONE and VOLUME. Touching the key clears the queue, as on a WinKeyer.

docs.title: Errors
docs.text: n SERIAL ERRORS on the screen counts the serial reads and writes that USB refused. A refused write drops the rest of its 64-byte piece. A full USB buffer is not an error: the device tries again on the next poll.

docs.title: Hardware reference
docs.text:
These pages describe the HamCube as PocketCW uses it. The Mini and the Pro run the same firmware, and the Pro adds the decoder board. The facts about the hardware and the vendor firmware were found by static analysis and emulation of vendor firmware V5.03. Addresses such as 0x080185E0 point into the vendor app image, which starts at 0x08005000.

PocketCW was tested on a Mini with board version 2.64 only. No Pro has been checked.

Not checked on a board. Likely Inferred. Not checked on a board. Role unknown The firmware drives the pin, but what the pin does is not known.
