docs.title: Signal path
docs.text:
PA8 makes the audio. It goes into input 1 of the audio codec, and the codec's analog bypass sends it to the speaker and the headphone jack. The speaker amplifier needs PB12 high.

  • The vendor sends a square wave on PA8 at the tone pitch, from TMR1 channel 1 PWM. Confirmed on 2.64.
  • PocketCW uses PA8 as a 1 bit DAC: a 281 kHz pulse train with a new duty on every pulse, for 17,578 samples a second. The codec input and the headphones smooth the pulses into sine tones and noise. Confirmed on 2.64.

PocketCW timing (firmware/src/audio.rs): TMR1 counts 256 steps per pulse at 72 MHz, which is 281.25 kHz. Each sample lasts 16 pulses.

  • At each TMR1 overflow, DMA2 channel 1 copies the next duty from a buffer of 32 pulses into the channel 1 compare register. The request reaches DMA2 through its flexible mapping, ID 0x37. The fixed mapping also wires TMR1 overflow to DMA1 channel 5, the decoder board link's receive channel, so DMA1 runs on flexible mapping too, with channel 5 on USART1 RX (ID 0x19).
  • The DMA interrupts at each half of the buffer. The sample interrupt then fills the half just played: one synth sample, as 16 duties.
  • Rounding a duty to a whole count leaves an error. logic/src/pwm.rs feeds each error into the next two pulses, so the rounding noise follows (1 - z^-1)^2 at the pulse rate, far above the audio band. Below 8 kHz the rounding noise is 46 to 48 dB under that of one duty held for the whole sample.
  • Between sounds the duty stays at half, the silent level, so a new sound does not pop. Once both halves of the buffer are silent, the DMA and the sample interrupt stop.

docs.title: Codecs
docs.text:
The board has one of two codecs on I2C2. PocketCW tries the ES8388 address first, then the WM8978 address, and uses the one that answers.

Codec I2C address Boards WM8978 0x1A Older boards. ES8388 0x10 Board 2.64, which has no device at 0x1A.

docs.title: WM8978
docs.text:
V5.03.13 uses the ALIENTEK WM8978 driver: register write at 0x0801BEE8, register cache at RAM 0x200000F0. Its setup at 0x08005F04 leaves these values:

Register Value Effect R0 0 Reset. R1 0x00B Bias on, VMID 5k. R2 0x000 Inputs and OUT1 off. R3 0x06C Output mixers and OUT2 on. R43 0x010 ROUT2 inverted, for the bridged speaker. R49 0x004 Speaker boost. R44 0x000 Nothing into the input PGAs. R47, R48 0x170 Line input into the boost stage at +6 dB. R50, R51 0x01E Bypass into the output mixers at +6 dB.

Then it drives PB12 high and sets the speaker volume, R54 and R55, from the vendor volume setting (0 to 63, and 0 writes the mute bit). R52 and R53, the OUT1 volume, are written at 0x080164D4, but R2 leaves OUT1 off.

PocketCW writes the same values (firmware/src/wm8978.rs). Its volume level 44 gives 61 in R54 and R55, which is +4 dB.

docs.title: ES8388
docs.text:
No published vendor firmware sets up the ES8388, so V5.03 and V5.03.13 are silent on board 2.64. Unpublished V5.03.15, shipped on some 2.64 units, has working sound. See Board variants.

PocketCW (firmware/src/es8388.rs) follows the bypass start-up in section 10.4 of the Everest ES8388 User Guide:

Step Register = value Effect 1 0x02 = 0xF3 State machines in reset, references down. 2 0x00 = 0x07 Reference on, VMID 5k. 3 0x01 = 0x40 Analog and bias generator on. 4 0x03 = 0x3F ADCs down, analog inputs on for the bypass. 5 0x04 = 0xFC DACs down; LOUT1, ROUT1, LOUT2 and ROUT2 on. 6 0x26 = 0x00 Mixer source: LIN1 and RIN1. 7 0x02 = 0xF0 References up. 8 Volume Registers 0x27 and 0x2A (input into the output mixers), and 0x2E to 0x31 (output volumes). 9 Wait 100 ms VMID charges. 10 0x00 = 0x05 VMID 50k for play.
  • Analog bypass from input 1 to the output mixers, with PB12 high, plays through the speaker. At 0 dB output volume it is very loud. Input 2 carries no tone.
  • OUT1 (LOUT1, ROUT1) drives the speaker, and OUT2 (LOUT2, ROUT2) the headphones.
  • A plug in the headphone jack cuts the speaker whatever the codec setup, so the jack switch is in the speaker path. The switch reaches no MCU input, so the firmware cannot tell which output is in use.

docs.title: Volume
docs.text:
logic/src/volume.rs maps the VOLUME setting. Level 0 mutes, and level 44 is +4.5 dB.

Output Level 1 Step ES8388 headphones (OUT2) -60 dB 1.5 dB ES8388 speaker (OUT1) -38.5 dB 1 dB WM8978 speaker and headphones -60 dB 1.5 dB
  • Through the speaker, a tone below about -39 dB is lost in a quiet room, and the headphones are still clear at -60 dB. The firmware cannot tell which output is in use, so it sets both.
  • The ES8388 output stage steps 1.5 dB. The synth makes the speaker's levels between those steps: it cuts the whole signal by 0 dB, 0.5 dB or 1 dB, easing over 5 ms so the change does not click. The headphones hear that cut too, so they land within 0.5 dB of their level.
  • On the ES8388, the output stage cuts first, down to -45 dB. Below that, the mixer input cuts in 3 dB steps. A cut before the output stage raises the hiss relative to the tone. The mixer feeds both outputs, and the speaker's output stage makes up its cut.
  • Through the speaker, a sine tone is clean at 0 dB and starts to sound harsh at +1.5 dB. Speech still sounds clean at +3 dB, since it reaches its peak far less often than a tone.
  • Each volume change pops on both outputs, also in silence and with PA8 floating, so the pop does not come from PA8. The ES8388's analog volume registers have no zero cross or soft ramp setting.

docs.title: Speaker amplifier
docs.text:
PB12 enables the speaker amplifier.

  • The vendor sets it high during WM8978 init, and toggles it with the mute shortcut.
  • PocketCW holds it low until the codec setup ends, which on the ES8388 includes the VMID charge. Then it drives PB12 high while the volume is above 0. At volume 0 the amplifier is off, so the pulse train on the codec input cannot reach the speaker.

docs.title: Synthesis
docs.text:
logic/src/synth.rs mixes five voices into one signal: your sidetone and four players, so stations can overlap.

  • Key edges rise and fall over 5 ms on a raised cosine, so they do not click.
  • WAVE SQUARE plays 7.5 dB under a sine's peak: at the same peak, it sounds 7.5 dB louder, by ear on the speaker and the headphones.
  • WAVE SQUARE sums the odd harmonics up to 31. At 17.6 kHz this reaches the Nyquist frequency for pitches down to 284 Hz. A lower pitch loses its top harmonics.
  • Band noise has a 500 Hz bandwidth, like a receiver CW filter. Its 10 levels are 2.5 dB apart, up to an RMS of 0.35.
  • Fading goes down to a tenth at the top level. Each player fades at its own rate, so stations fade apart.
  • When stations overlap, the gain drops so the sum stays at one voice's peak. The gain recovers over 0.5 s, like a receiver AGC. A limiter above 0.8 bends noise peaks down so the mix does not clip.

docs.title: The reading
docs.text: PA1 is ADC1 channel 1: the battery through a 2:1 divider, read against the 3.3 V supply. PocketCW also reads the internal 1.2 V reference on channel 17, which gives the supply voltage the ADC measures against. Each reading averages 8 samples at the longest sample time.

docs.title: Vendor behavior
docs.text:
V5.03.13 shows battery volts as counts times 0.0016169, for a 2500 mAh cell, and never reads a charge status. Confirmed.

Counts Volts Vendor icon 2037 3.29 1 segment 2345 3.79 2 segments 2400 3.88 3 segments 2470 3.99 4 segments below 1768 2.86 Shuts down

docs.title: PocketCW gauge
docs.text:
logic/src/battery.rs uses the vendor scale, but divider and regulator tolerances move the scale by a few percent on each unit. So the gauge learns each unit's reading at full charge and scales to it.

Rule Value Full cell 4.2 V, about 2597 counts at the vendor scale. Learned full point Within about 3 % of the design value. It takes a reading higher than the old full point, once 120 s have passed with no USB power, so charger surface charge has gone. Saved at 0x780. USB detect At startup, a reading 75 counts or more above the full point. Later, a jump of 60 counts or more up (USB in) or down (USB out) in one poll. With USB in, PA1 reads about 4.5 % above a full cell. Percent From a curve for a lithium cell under light load: 0 % at 3.4 V, 50 % near 3.82 V, 100 % at 4.2 V. Low Below 3.4 V, off USB. The status line says BATTERY LOW: PLUG IN USB, and the icon shows a red outline. Empty Below 3.2 V, or a supply below 3.1 V, for 10 polls in a row. The status line says BATTERY EMPTY: POWERING OFF, and 2 s later the device saves and powers off.

The UI polls the battery once a second.

When the regulator drops out, the supply falls with the battery, and a reading against the supply stays steady. A supply reading under 98 % of the highest seen marks a dropout. The gauge then scales the battery reading by the supply ratio. The ratio of two reference readings cancels the reference's own error.

None of the low and empty behavior has been checked on a board with a draining battery.

docs.title: Board variants
docs.text:
The board version is in option bytes Data0 and Data1. The vendor System Information screen shows it as (Data0 - 0xF0).(Data1 in hex): F2 60 is 2.60. The 2.64 unit reads Data1 = 0x64.

PocketCW was tested on board 2.64 only.

docs.title: What the vendor firmware reads
docs.text:
Vendor V5.03.13 runs on every board from 2.60. It reads the board version in three places only:

What Where Rule LCD init 0x08014F7A reads Data1 IPS init (0x080177E6) when Data1 == 0x63, ILI9341 init (0x080134F4) otherwise. Key output 0x08009F86, 0x0800A5E6 and 0x08013EE8 compare Data0 and Data1 with F2 60 PA3, the func jack ring, is driven only on 2.60. PA2 and the PB2 LED are driven on every board. System Information 0x0800C300 copies Data0 and Data1 to RAM 0x2000095C Display only.

V5.03.13 knows only the WM8978 codec. So a board with an ES8388, such as 2.64, is silent under it. A 2.64 unit shipped with unpublished V5.03.15 had working sound, so V5.03.15 sets up the ES8388. No dump of V5.03.15 exists yet.

Data1 does not reliably name the panel. The activation routine writes F2 60 on every board, so an activated IPS board can read 2.60.

docs.title: What PocketCW does
docs.text: What PocketCW Panel Asks the panel for its ID first, then uses Data1. F2 at power on overrides both. See Display. Codec Uses the codec that answers on I2C: 0x10 for the ES8388, 0x1A for the WM8978. See Audio. Func jack Drives PA2 and PA3 on every board. See Key and func jacks. System screen Shows the board version, the panel type, and where the panel choice came from.

docs.title: Known differences
docs.text: Part Older boards Board 2.63 Board 2.64 Panel ILI9341 compatible ST7789 style IPS ST7789 style IPS Codec WM8978 at 0x1A Not known ES8388 at 0x10

docs.title: Buttons
docs.text:
The device has four buttons, F1 to F4, and a dial that turns and clicks. See Pins for the pins.

Input Pin Level F1 to F4 PA4 to PA7 Active high, internal pull-down. Dial left, dial right PC14, PC15 Active high, internal pull-down. Dial click PA0 Active high. Also the standby wakeup pin.

The dial click also closes the dial left contact: PC14 reads high while PA0 is pressed.

docs.title: PocketCW timing
docs.text:
logic/src/buttons.rs reads every input once per millisecond, in the tick task.

Rule Value Debounce 8 ms. Press event Sent at the press, without waiting for release. Dial repeat While the dial stays turned: a repeat after 400 ms, then every 80 ms. Dial click hold 1000 ms; the vendor uses 1500 ms. Release after the hold turns the device off. A button press or dial turn before the release cancels it. Dial left after a click Ignored while the click is down and for 50 ms after it opens.

The click that wakes the device is still down when the app starts. logic/src/input.rs ignores that click until it is released.

The F buttons also send a hold event after 500 ms. Input turns an F press into SoftDown, the hold into SoftHold, and the release into Soft, the short action. The UI skips the release of a key whose press or hold already acted. A press that Input did not map, such as one that skipped the boot screen or cancelled a power off, maps nothing at its hold or release.

docs.title: Panel override at power on
docs.text: F2 held at power on, for the first 50 ms that the app reads it, picks the other screen type. See Display.

docs.title: Decoder board
docs.text:
The Pro model adds a decoder board that listens to a radio's audio. The vendor V5.03 app image starts at 0x08005000. No Pro unit has been checked.

The host needs three things to use the board: power on PB13, the USART1 link, and the tone line on PB14.

docs.title: Power (PB13)
docs.text:
• Push-pull output (HAL_GPIO_Init at 0x0801560A and 0x08015618). Confirmed.
  • Driven low at boot, with PB2, PB7, PB12 and PB15 (0x08015598). Confirmed.
  • After the settings load, set from the "decoder board power" setting (0x08013244). The menu toggle near 0x08009F9E drives it high for ON and low for OFF. OFF also clears the board present flags. So high = board powered. Confirmed.

docs.title: Link (USART1)
docs.text:
• Setup at 0x08015858. 115200 baud, 8N1, TX and RX. PA9 TX is alternate function push-pull (0x080128C2), PA10 RX is an input (0x080128D2). Confirmed.
  • RX goes by DMA1 channel 5 into a 64 byte buffer. The idle line interrupt (0x08018C44) ends a frame, so frames need no terminator. Confirmed.
  • The frame parser is at 0x08005D00, called from 0x0801727C. Host frames end with \r\n. Confirmed.

docs.title: Board to host
docs.text:
Every frame starts with RE+ (string at 0x08022867), then a two letter code. Confirmed.

Frame Host action RE+IF1x Marks the board present and replies AT+OK\r\n. x = 1 sets a second flag whose use is unknown. RE+MD0, RE+MD1 Stores the digit. Use unknown. RE+FL0 to RE+FL2 Stores the filter setting. The vendor shows it as an icon. RE+NR0 to RE+NR6 Stores the noise reduction level. The vendor shows it as an icon. RE+MC, RE+AC, RE+MU, RE+VL Accepted, no action. Any other RE+ frame Replies AT+ERR\r\n.

PocketCW (logic/src/board.rs) follows the same rules. A known code with a digit out of range changes nothing. A frame without RE+ gets no reply, as in the vendor parser. Confirmed in code.

docs.title: Host to board
docs.text:
Sent through 0x0801D480, which formats and transmits. Confirmed.

Command When AT+FL<0..2> (0x0800BD7C) F2 on the decoder screen cycles the filter. AT+NR<0..6> (0x0800BD8C) F3 on the decoder screen cycles noise reduction. AT+VL<000..063> (0x080183BC, 0x0801B120) The host volume changed and the board is present. The value has three digits.

docs.title: Detection
docs.text: The host never asks. The board sends RE+IF1x, and the host answers AT+OK. Confirmed in code. That the board sends it at power up is Likely.

docs.title: Decoding
docs.text:
The board sends no characters. It raises PB14 while it hears a tone, and the host times and decodes the marks itself. Setup at 0x08006410 sets PB14 as an input with pull-down. The 1 ms SysTick polls it (0x080179CC calls 0x0800A094; high goes to 0x0801D6D4, low to 0x0801D71C). Confirmed.

The board manual describes no audio path from the board into the host, and the host gets no audio from it, only PB14.

docs.title: Vendor decoding rules
docs.text:
At 0x0801D6D4 and 0x0801D71C. Times are in 1 ms samples. Start values: unit 51, word 154, 20 WPM.

  • Up to 6 low samples inside a tone do not end it. A mark lasts the high run plus 6.
  • A mark under 0.5 unit is not an element. It pulls the unit down by a quarter of the difference, and a unit under 24 resets to 51.
  • A mark from 0.5 to under 1.5 units is a dot. A longer mark is a dash, and sets word = (word + mark) / 2, held to 77 to 365, WPM = 3850 / word, unit = word / 3.
  • A gap over 2 units ends the character. A gap over 1.5 words gives one word space. A 9th element clears the pattern.

docs.title: Ports
docs.text:
From the decoder board user manual and the Quick Start Guide. Confirmed in the manuals.

Port Use AUX1 Radio audio in, or the external MIC module. The board filters this and detects tone in it. AUX2 Stereo headphone or powered speaker out. AT+VL sets its volume from the host volume. AUX3 Not used. USB The Pro's charging port. No vendor code refers to it.

docs.title: PocketCW
docs.text:
All of this is confirmed in code and not on a board.

  • The DECODER BOARD setting, in the DEVICE section, defaults to OFF, so a Mini sees no change. ON powers the board, starts USART1, and adds RADIO to the menu.
  • OFF stops USART1, sets PA9 as a pulled-down input so the board is not powered through it, and drives PB13 low. PA10 has a pull-up, so an idle line reads high with no board.
  • Frames are parsed in the USART1 interrupt and get the vendor replies at once.
  • The RADIO screen shows the board state, the filter and noise reduction (F2 and F3 send AT+FL and AT+NR), the heard speed, and the decoded text.
  • A volume change sends AT+VL once the board has announced itself. The value is the WM8978 speaker register for the same volume, 0 to 63.
  • PB14 is polled every 1 ms while the RADIO screen is open, and on every screen while USB OUT is RADIO.
  • The baud rate comes from the crystal. The divider error is 0.16 %.
  • Frames with framing, noise or overrun errors count as ERR n on the RADIO screen.

docs.title: PocketCW decoding
docs.text:
logic/src/listen.rs decodes in its own way. The vendor rules cannot follow below about 10 WPM, count the bridged silence into every mark, and let a noise blip pull the speed down.

  • A dropout of 6 ms or less inside a mark is bridged, and the mark keeps its true length. A mark under 10 ms is noise.
  • Speed: two adjacent marks 2 to 4.5 times apart are a dot and a dash. The first pair sets the speed. A sample more than 1.5 times off the estimate replaces it, and other samples average in at 1/8. The range is 5 to 60 WPM.
  • The marks of a character are classified when the character ends, at the midpoint of the dot and dash estimates.
  • A character ends after 2 dots of silence. A word ends after 5 dots, or after 5/3 of the learned letter gap when that is longer, so Farnsworth spacing decodes. The letter gap is learned from adjacent gaps, the same way as the speed.
  • WPM = 1200 / dot length in ms.
  • Tests key known text and require it back: 5 to 60 WPM, 20 % jitter, dash ratios 2.5 and 3.5, Farnsworth 20/8 and 18/10, speed changes up to 3 times, pauses, dropouts, blips and noise bursts. The vendor test inputs are kept, with the sent text as the expected output.

The same decoder reads your keying in STRAIGHT mode.

docs.title: Display
docs.text: The LCD is 320 x 240 in landscape, RGB565 (COLMOD 0x55). It is on SPI1, which it shares with the SPI flash. See Pins.

docs.title: Two panel types
docs.text:
Panel Boards MADCTL Vendor init ILI9341 compatible Older boards 0xE8 0x080145E4 in V5.03, 0x080134F4 in V5.03.13 ST7789 style IPS Board 2.63 and later, 2.64 too 0xA0 0x080177E6 in V5.03.13

V5.03.13 sends the IPS init only when Data1 == 0x63, with a beq at 0x08014F80. So under V5.03.13, board 2.64 gets the ILI9341 init.

With the wrong init, the image turns 90 degrees and wraps into interlaced strips. The ILI9341 init sends C0h 0x23 (power control 1). On the ST7789, C0h is LCMCTRL, and 0x23 sets its XMV bit, which swaps the row and column address order. That gives the rotation and the strips.

firmware/src/lcd.rs holds both init sequences, from V5.03.13.

docs.title: Bus setup
docs.text:
• The vendor sets LCD CS, LCD DC, flash CS and LCD reset to large drive, and SPI SCK and MOSI to maximum drive. PocketCW does the same.
  • The vendor raises CS after every command and parameter byte. PocketCW does the same, but sends pixel data in one burst.
  • SPI1 runs at 18 MHz for both panels: APB2 / 4 in the vendor (HAL init at 0x08015ED8), APB2 / 2 in PocketCW.

docs.title: How PocketCW picks the panel
docs.text:
Data1 does not reliably name the panel. The vendor activation routine writes F2 60 on every board, so an activated IPS board can read 2.60 and get the ILI9341 init, under the vendor firmware and under PocketCW.

PocketCW picks the panel in this order (logic/src/panel.rs):

  1. A choice saved with F2 at power on.
  2. The panel's ID.
  3. Data1: IPS from 0x63 up, except 0xFF (an erased byte), which gets the ILI9341, as in the vendor firmware.

docs.title: ID read
docs.text:
After the reset pulse, PocketCW bit-bangs RDDID (0x04) and reads 32 bits on both PB4 and PB5. A panel answers on its SDO pin if one is wired, and on its bidirectional SDA pin otherwise. Each read runs twice, once with the pins pulled up and once pulled down. A pin whose 24 ID bits differ between the two reads is not driven. The dummy bit and the 7 bits after the ID can float, so they are left out of the check.

The ST7789V answer 85 85 52, right after the one dummy clock that both datasheets document, picks IPS. An ILI9341 answers 00 80 00, or a module maker's ID with ID2 at 0x80 or more, so it cannot match. No ILI9341 ID is matched, because its D3h read is not documented for the serial interface.

The SYSTEM screen shows the raw 32 bits read pulled up for each pin, or FLOAT. On the 2.64 Mini, B4 reads 42C2A97F: a dummy 0, the ID 85 85 52, and 7 floating ones. B5 is FLOAT.

docs.title: F2 override
docs.text:
Hold F2 while the board powers on, and PocketCW uses the other panel type. It saves the choice in its own EEPROM record at 0x7B0. Hold F2 at power on again to go back. A choice that matches the automatic one is saved as no choice.

The BOARD row of the SYSTEM screen shows where the choice came from:

Label Source ID The panel's ID. AUTO Data1. SET The saved choice. NOSAVE F2 was held, but the EEPROM write failed. The flip still applies until power off.

docs.title: Memory read
docs.text:
Screenshots need the panel to send its memory back with RAMRD (0x2E). Neither datasheet fixes the serial framing: the dummy bits before the data, 2 or 3 bytes a pixel, and the channel order.

On the 2.64 Mini (IPS panel), the panel answers on PB4 with one dummy byte, then 3 bytes a pixel in RGB order, each channel in the top 6 bits. Pulled up and pulled down agree, so PB4 is driven; PB5 reads all ones. Because the dummy is a whole byte, SPI1 can read the memory with MISO on PB4. Red and blue come back with a sixth bit the host never wrote: written 0xF800 reads F8 00 00, and 0x07E0 reads 04 FC 04. Confirmed on 2.64. The ILI9341 panel is not checked.

The hardware probe writes 8 known pixels at the top left, then bit-bangs RAMRD on PB4 and PB5, once pulled up and once pulled down. panel::find_framing searches 0 to 16 skipped bits, RGB565 and RGB666, and RGB and BGR order for the framing that gives the pixels back. The last two rows of the probe show, for each pin:

Item Meaning up, dn The framing found with the pin pulled up and pulled down, as skipped bits / format / order, such as 9/666/RGB. NONE when no framing gives the pixels back. Hex The first 64 bits read pulled up.

The same framing pulled up and pulled down on one pin means the panel drives that pin, and screenshots can use it.

docs.title: Backlight
docs.text: PB8 drives the backlight from TMR4 channel 3, PWM at 20 kHz. PocketCW holds it off until the first screen clear, because the panel shows random pixels before that.

docs.title: Layout
docs.text:
Region Contents MCU 0x08000000 to 0x08004FFF The vendor bootloader. Never write here. MCU 0x08005000 up The app. The app must set VTOR to 0x08005000. SPI flash 0x000000 to 0x025FFF Vendor boot screen, file F000000.bin. SPI flash 0x030000 to 0x0C5FFF Vendor UI images, file F0000C0.bin. SPI flash 0x100000 up PocketCW content pack, file F000400.bin, up to 8,372,224 bytes. SPI flash 0xE00000 to 0xFECFFF Vendor fonts, file F003800.bin.

The vendor ranges are the used 4 KB sectors in a scan of a 2.64 unit. Every other sector read blank: 0x026000 to 0x02FFFF, 0x0C6000 to 0xDFFFFF, and 0xFED000 to 0xFFFFFF.

PocketCW runs from the MCU app area and reads the content pack from the SPI flash.

tools/pack/pack.py builds F000400.bin; logic/src/pack.rs gives the format. tools/release.sh builds it into each release.

firmware/memory.x gives the app 236 KB from 0x08005000, and cortex-m-rt sets VTOR from its set-vtor feature.

docs.title: Update files
docs.text: An update file name is a hex offset in KB, after a letter: A for MCU flash, F for SPI flash. A000014.bin is MCU flash plus 0x14 KB, which is 0x08005000.

docs.title: The bootloader
docs.text:
The bootloader is a modified Artery virtual_msc_iap demo. It shows a USB drive: "HAM MODULE" in the vendor manual, "POKEMON-2" on board 2.64.

To start it: hold F1 and F4, then hold the dial until the update screen shows. Plug in USB after that.

The bootloader routes file data by the name in the root directory entry. So the directory entry must reach the device before the data, as Windows writes it. macOS and mtools write the data first, and the data goes to the wrong place.

On macOS, PocketCW installs with tools/pocketcw-flash.c. The tool blocks the mount of the update drive, so macOS writes nothing to it. Then it writes the raw disk in the order the bootloader needs: directory entry, data, FAT, directory entry again.

The update drive is FAT16 with 2 KB sectors, 8 KB clusters and 51,200 sectors (100 MB). Confirmed on 2.64; pocketcw-flash prints the cluster size. pocketcw-flash writes the whole FAT in one sector, so a file holds at most 1022 clusters: 8,372,224 bytes.

An SPI flash install erases and programs the 4 KB sectors its file covers. Confirmed on 2.64 with a 2,093,056 byte file at 0x100000, the largest tested: every sector of it read back. A 5.97 MB content pack also installed and played to its last clip, and an 8.37 MB one installed and played its first and last clips. Tags written beforehand in the sector just past its end, 4 KB, 64 KB and 1 MB past it, and at 0xC00000 and 0xDFF000 all survived.

Drive writes that are not part of an update file can also land in the SPI flash. On 2.64, after a session with several installs, 0x101000 to 0x103FFF held a FAT directory cluster (first entry ., attribute 0x12) in place of the test file data. The sectors were erased before the write. Likely: macOS wrote to the drive while it was mounted, and the bootloader routed the write to the SPI flash beside the last F file. So data that PocketCW keeps in the SPI flash checks its own frames, and the install path never lets macOS mount the drive.

After a finished write, the status file reads Success for about 1 second. Then the drive drops off USB and comes back as Ready.

A failed write leaves the bootloader in update mode at every power on, until a write finishes. The vendor upgrade notes say so, and a 2.64 unit did it. Likely cause on that unit: macOS mounted the drive when it came back Ready after Success, and wrote its own files to it. So the tool counts a write as done only when it reads Success, and it blocks the mount until the drive is back.

On first installs, every user who installed only A000014.bin saw the device stay in update mode. Installing an F file first, then A000014.bin, fixed it. The vendor V5.03 notes give the same fix for a failed upgrade: F000000.bin, then A000014.bin. The cause is not known; no dump of the bootloader exists. So a first install writes F000400.bin, the content pack, before A000014.bin. The install script asks whether to write it, since an update needs it only when the pack changed. The stock install always writes F0000C0.bin before A000014.bin. pocketcw-flash writes both files in one update mode session, as a Windows copy does: after Success on the F file, it waits for the drive to come back Ready, then writes the A file. A retry starts again at the F file.

docs.title: Write protection
docs.text:
The vendor app has a one-time activation routine at 0x08018014, keyed to the chip UID. It writes these option bytes: Data0 and Data1 = F2 60, WRP0 = 0xE0, EOPB0 = 0xFE, Data3 and Data4 = D, y.

WRP0 = 0xE0 write-protects 0x08000000 to 0x08004FFF exactly. So on an activated unit, a flash write cannot overwrite the bootloader.

At every boot, the vendor app checks Data3 and Data4. If they do not hold D, y, the app overwrites itself with random data. PocketCW does not need these bytes. They matter only when the vendor firmware must run after an option byte erase.

docs.title: Key jack
docs.text:
The key jack, labeled "key", takes a paddle, a straight key or a sideswiper.

Contact Pin Level Tip PB1 Active low, internal pull-up. Ring PB0 Active low, internal pull-up.
  • The vendor default treats PB0 as dit. On the paddle of the 2.64 unit, PB0 is dah and PB1 is dit, so that unit needed the vendor swap setting. Confirmed on 2.64.
  • PocketCW with PADDLES NORMAL puts dits on the tip (PB1). STRAIGHT mode keys from either contact, so a sideswiper works. Confirmed in code.
  • In the vendor keyboard mode, the same pins carry the PS/2 clock and data, with EXTI0 on PB0. Confirmed.

PocketCW rules for each contact, in logic/src/keyer.rs. Confirmed in code.

Rule Value Why Debounce 8 ms Contacts bounce for up to about 6 to 10 ms. 8 ms is under half the 20 ms dot at 60 WPM. Closed at power on Does not key until it opens. A mono plug, or a key held at power on, does not key. Ring closed 5 s Stops keying until it opens. A mono plug shorts the ring. 5 s is longer than the longest character, 0 at 5 WPM. Tip closed 30 s Stops keying until it opens. Leaves time to hold a straight key down to tune a radio.

docs.title: Func jack
docs.text:
The func jack, labeled "func", keys a radio or an external keyer.

Contact Pin Level Tip PA2 High = closed. Ring PA3 High = closed.
  • The vendor drives PA2 on every board, and PA3 only on board 2.60. Confirmed.
  • PocketCW drives both on every board. With OUT TYPE STRAIGHT, one line follows the keyer output. With OUT TYPE PADDLE, the two lines follow the dit and dah contacts. OUT LINES swaps tip and ring. KEY OUT OFF holds both open. Confirmed in code.
  • A memory keys the func jack only with OUT TYPE STRAIGHT, because PADDLE output follows the contacts and not the keyer. Confirmed in code.

docs.title: LED
docs.text: PB2 drives the output LED, active high. The vendor lights it during every sent element, and the bootloader blinks it. PocketCW lights it while the keyer output or a memory keys. Confirmed on 2.64.

docs.title: The chip
docs.text:
• Artery AT32F403A, 48 pins, 256 KB flash. The flash size register at 0x1FFFF7E0 reads 256. The debug IDCODE is 0x70050242.
  • RAM is 96 KB for this part family. PocketCW uses 64 KB until the size is checked.
  • The 96 bit unique ID at 0x1FFFF7E8 shows on the SYSTEM screen.

docs.title: Option bytes
docs.text:
On the 2.64 unit, the low bytes from 0x1FFFF800 up read A5 FF F2 64 E0 FF FF FF FE FF 44 79.

  • FAP = 0xA5, so flash read protection is off. A running app or an SWD probe can read the bootloader.
  • Data0 and Data1 hold the board version. See Board variants.
  • WRP0 = 0xE0 write-protects the bootloader. See Flash layout and bootloader.
  • EOPB0 = 0xFE. It likely selects 224 KB of SRAM with 128 KB of zero wait flash, 0x08000000 to 0x08020000; this is not checked against Artery's documents. Code past 0x08020000 runs much slower: the sample interrupt measured 2661 cycles with its code there and 1092 with it inside the first 128 KB, on board 2.64. firmware/memory.x puts the .fast_text section right after the vector table for this.

PocketCW reads Data1 at 0x1FFFF806.

docs.title: Clock
docs.text:
The board has an 8 MHz crystal (HEXT).

  • The vendor app runs the PLL from the crystal times 9, for 72 MHz (SystemClock_Config at 0x080185E0, HSE_VALUE 8 MHz at 0x08010E38). It hangs when the crystal does not start within 100 ms (0x0801861C). So every board that runs the vendor firmware has a working crystal.
  • The vendor firmware is built with Keil MDK on the ST STM32F1 HAL, with the medium density startup file and soft float. Its timer prescalers assume 72 MHz.
  • The clock source that the bootloader leaves running is not known.

PocketCW (firmware/src/clock.rs) also runs at 72 MHz.

  1. It switches to the internal 8 MHz clock (HICK) while it sets up the PLL.
  2. It starts the crystal, then runs the PLL from HEXT / 2 times 18. Each start has 100 ms.
  3. If the crystal or the PLL does not start, it runs the PLL from HICK / 2 times 18.
  4. If that fails too, it stays on HICK at 8 MHz.

APB1 and APB2 run at 36 MHz. Timers on these buses run at 72 MHz.

The CLOCK row of the SYSTEM screen reads the PLL source back from CFG.PLLRCS: XTAL, or HICK in red as a fault.

docs.title: Debug access
docs.text:
• The vendor app sets AFIO MAPR SWJ_CFG to 111 at 0x08011054. This likely turns SWD off while the vendor app runs, so a probe would need connect under reset.
  • PocketCW sets SWJ_CFG to 010: JTAG off, SWD on. This frees PA15, PB3 and PB4. It also remaps SPI1 to PB3, PB4 and PB5.

docs.title: Pins
docs.text:
firmware/src/pins.rs names every pin. The vendor firmware uses the same pins from board 2.60.

Pin Name in pins.rs Function Status PA0 POWER_BUTTON Dial click, the power button. Active high. The vendor sets PA0 as the standby wakeup pin before power off. PC14 also reads high while the dial is pressed. Confirmed on 2.64 PA1 BATTERY ADC1 channel 1: the battery through a 2:1 divider, read against the 3.3 V supply. See Battery. Confirmed PA2 KEY_OUT_TIP Func jack tip, keyed output, high = closed. Keys a radio's or keyer's dit input, or a straight key input. Confirmed on 2.64 PA3 KEY_OUT_RING Func jack ring, keyed output, high = closed. With PA2 it passes paddle contacts to an external keyer: dit on PA2, dah on PA3. The vendor drives PA3 only on board 2.60. Confirmed on 2.64 PA4, PA5, PA6, PA7 F_KEYS F1, F2, F3, F4. Active high, internal pull-down. Confirmed on 2.64 PA8 SIDETONE Audio, TMR1 channel 1. See Audio. Confirmed on 2.64 PA9, PA10 DECODER_TX, DECODER_RX USART1 TX and RX to the decoder board, DMA on RX. Confirmed PA11, PA12 none USB device. Confirmed (USB peripheral in use) PA15 LCD_RESET LCD reset. Confirmed PB0 RING Key jack ring. Active low, internal pull-up. See Key and func jacks. Confirmed on 2.64 PB1 TIP Key jack tip. Active low, internal pull-up. Confirmed on 2.64 PB2 LED Output LED, active high. Confirmed on 2.64 PB3, PB4, PB5 LCD_SCK, LCD_MISO, LCD_MOSI SPI1 SCK, MISO and MOSI, remapped. The LCD and the SPI flash share the bus. Confirmed PB6 LCD_CS LCD chip select. Confirmed PB7 LCD_DC LCD data or command, low = command. Confirmed PB8 BACKLIGHT LCD backlight, TMR4 channel 3 PWM at 20 kHz, duty 0 to 100. Confirmed PB9 FLASH_CS SPI flash chip select. Read command 0x03, 24 bit address. Confirmed PB10, PB11 I2C_SCL, I2C_SDA I2C2 SCL and SDA, to the EEPROM and the audio codec. PocketCW drives them in software at about 65 kHz. Confirmed PB12 SPEAKER_AMP Speaker amplifier enable. See Audio. Confirmed PB13 DECODER_POWER Decoder board power, high = on. See Decoder board. Confirmed in code PB14 DECODER_TONE Decoder board tone detect, high while the board hears a tone. Input, pull-down. Confirmed in code PB15 PB15 Output. The vendor drives it low at boot (0x08015598) and again after LCD init. PocketCW drives it low at boot. Role unknown PC13 POWER_HOLD Power hold, high = stay on. See Power. Confirmed on 2.64 PC14, PC15 DIAL_LEFT, DIAL_RIGHT Dial left and dial right. Active high, internal pull-down. Confirmed on 2.64

Without the pull-ups, the key jack inputs float and read at random.

docs.title: Power on
docs.text:
A dial click (PA0) powers the board up. PC13 is the power hold, high = stay on. Unless the app drives PC13 high, power drops about 1 s later, with the power-on reset flag set and the backup registers cleared. Confirmed on 2.64.

The vendor app sets PC13 high first at boot. PocketCW does the same in power::hold, right after the GPIO clocks start.

docs.title: Power off
docs.text:
The vendor long press, over 1.5 s on PA0, does this in order:

  1. Stops the backlight PWM and drives PB2 low.
  2. Saves the settings.
  3. Drives PC13 low.
  4. Sets the speaker volume and drives PB12 low.
  5. Enters standby: PWR clock on, standby flag cleared, PA0 wakeup pin on, wakeup flag cleared, PDDS and SLEEPDEEP set, WFI.

PocketCW (power::standby) waits until the dial click reads released for 8 ms, because the wakeup pin wakes the chip at once while PA0 is high. Then it drives the backlight, the speaker amplifier, the LED, both func jack lines and PC13 low, and enters standby the same way. Before WFI it disables and clears every interrupt in the NVIC, because an enabled pending interrupt ends WFI even with interrupts masked. If standby is refused, the chip resets.

Before standby, PocketCW saves the settings, the memories, the letter statistics and the current practice session. A failed save shows on the status line for 3 s.

docs.title: Wake
docs.text: A dial click wakes the chip through reset. The bootloader starts the app again, and the app must drive PC13 high to stay on. The standby flag always reads clear when the app starts, so the app cannot tell a wake from standby from a cold start.

docs.title: Fault screen
docs.text:
On a panic, a hard fault or an unexpected interrupt, firmware/src/fault.rs:

  1. Drives both func jack lines and the LED low, so a radio does not stay keyed.
  2. Stops the PA8 audio output.
  3. Shows the fault on a dark red screen: the return addresses of a panic (see Panic screen), the PC, LR, CFSR, HFSR and BFAR values of a hard fault, or the number of an unexpected interrupt.
  4. Waits, with interrupts off, for a dial click, then enters standby.

docs.title: EEPROM
docs.text:
A 24C16 EEPROM sits on I2C2 at 0x50: 2 KB, as eight 256 byte blocks at addresses 0x50 to 0x57, with 16 byte pages.

The vendor firmware uses 0x000 to 0x367. PocketCW keeps its records above that (firmware/src/store.rs):

Address Record Magic 0x400 Letter statistics and Koch level Rl 0x480 Practice history: 32 slots of 12 bytes none 0x600 Memories Rm 0x700 Settings, copy 0 Rw 0x740 Settings, copy 1 Rw 0x780 Battery full point Rb 0x7A0 Boot count Rc 0x7B0 Panel choice Rp 0x7C0 up Free

Each record owns the bytes up to the next address, and startup reads all of them. So a longer record from later firmware still reads whole. Asserts in store.rs stop the build when a record grows into the next one.

docs.title: Record frame
docs.text:
logic/src/record.rs defines the frame:

Bytes Field 2 Magic 1 Version 1 Body length n Body 2 CRC-16/CCITT-FALSE of everything before it, high byte first

A reader takes the fields it knows from the front of the body. So later firmware can add fields at the end, and this firmware still reads the record. The version changes only when the body no longer starts the same way.

  • History slots are not frames. Each 12 byte slot ends in an 8 bit checksum.
  • Settings have two copies, saved in turn. Each copy ends its body with a save count, so a save cut off by power loss leaves the other copy to load.
  • The boot count record fits in one EEPROM page, so the write at every startup cannot tear it.
  • Records from before frames still read. Their magics are in capitals, and they end in an 8 bit checksum. A board that goes back to v0.1.0 after this firmware wrote its records sees blank records and uses defaults.

docs.title: Read failures
docs.text: When a read fails at startup, PocketCW starts with defaults for that record and refuses every write until the next power on. A write could otherwise replace a good record with defaults. The EEPROM row of the SYSTEM screen then shows FAIL.

docs.title: SPI flash
docs.text:
A GigaDevice GD25Q128 (JEDEC ID C8 40 18), 16 MB, on SPI1 with the screen: FLASH_CS PB9, LCD_CS PB6, MISO PB4. Confirmed on 2.64 with firmware/src/bin/flashprobe.rs. See Flash layout and bootloader for what lives where.

  • Status registers 1 to 3 read 00 00 40. No block protection: BP 0, CMP 0, WPS 0.
  • SFDP 1.0, with a 9 dword basic table. It lists 4 KB (0x20), 32 KB (0x52) and 64 KB (0xD8) erase, and no erase times or page size. Pages are 256 bytes.
  • Reads match at 18 MHz and at 4.5 MHz.
  • Erasing a 4 KB sector takes 15 ms when it is blank and 45 ms after it was programmed.
  • Programming a 256 byte page takes at most 917 µs, with the transfer at 18 MHz.
  • One page programmed in 16 pieces of 16 bytes reads back whole. So small records can go into a page one at a time.

firmware/src/spi_flash.rs is the driver: read 0x03, page program 0x02, 4 KB erase 0x20, JEDEC ID 0x9F, SFDP 0x5A, status 0x05, 0x35 and 0x15. The LCD changes the SPI1 divider and PB4, so every flash command sets both. The app reads the content pack (firmware/src/pack.rs) and writes nothing.

docs.title: No clock
docs.text: The board has no real-time clock. The date and time are lost at power off.

docs.title: Vendor firmware
docs.text: PocketCW does not include or need any vendor file. This page records what is known about the vendor firmware, for comparison and for going back to stock. See Go back to the stock firmware.

docs.title: Resource formats
docs.text:
• Images: an Image2Lcd header of 8 bytes (10 10, width as big endian 16 bits, height as big endian 16 bits, 01 1B), then RGB565 big endian, row major. This is the byte order the ILI9341 expects. Code refers to an image as 0xC0000000 | spi_flash_address.
  • Fonts (F003800.bin): starts with the text This is an image as font!, then a table of (width, height) byte pairs. Not decoded further. PocketCW uses its own font format. See Fonts.

docs.title: Why the vendor buttons feel slow
docs.text:
1. Buttons use the multi_button library with only single click and long press handlers. The tick runs every 11 ms. A click is reported about 110 ms after release. A second press inside that window becomes a double click, which has no handler, so the press is lost.
  2. The UI loops clear all key flags before and after each redraw, so a press during a redraw is lost.
  3. Images are read from SPI flash one byte at a time, without DMA, on the bus the LCD also uses. This makes redraws slow.

Paddle keying runs in the 1 ms SysTick interrupt, so the UI never delays it.

PocketCW sends a button event at the press, and reads buttons in its 1 ms tick. See Buttons.

docs.title: Vendor modes and settings
docs.text:
• Training: CW Memory, Code Listen, Koch Listen, Code Send, Followme, Chinese Code, Send Game, Listen Game.
  • Settings: F1 to F8 hotkey text, callsign, backlight, volume, decode lock and tolerance, auto shutdown, language, factory reset, date and time, key type (Auto, Hand, KeyB, Bug), Iambic A or B, dit and dah swap, tone, long and short code, decoder board power, Chinese decode, repeat group and interval, contact log (entry, view, ADIF export, init).

The vendor settings live at EEPROM 0x000 to 0x367. PocketCW never writes there, so the stock settings are still there after you go back. See Storage.

docs.title: User manual
docs.text: This manual tells you how to install PocketCW and how to use it.

docs.title: Install and recover
docs.text:

docs.title: Use the device
docs.text:
• Controls and power: the buttons, the dial, power on and off, and what the device saves.
  • Keys and jacks: paddles, straight keys, sideswipers, and the radio output.
  • USB keyboard: type what you key on a computer, or key VBand.
  • Menu: every screen the menu opens.
  • Keyer: the main screen.
  • Memories: store four messages and send them on your radio.
  • Timing: a close look at your keying.
  • Receive drills: Koch, words, callsigns, and the content pack drills NINJA and HEAD.
  • Ragchew: copy a full QSO between two stations.
  • Activate a park or summit: work a pileup of hunters.
  • Hunt: work activators on parks and summits.
  • Letters: your accuracy for each character.
  • Progress: practice time and totals.
  • Settings: every setting and its values.
  • System: version, hardware checks and battery.
  • Radio: the decoder board of the Pro model.
  • Status messages: what each message on the status line means.

docs.title: Terms
docs.text:
This manual uses these ham radio terms.

Term Meaning WPM Words per minute. The standard word is PARIS, so one dot lasts 1200 / WPM milliseconds. Dot, dash The short and the long element. A dash is 3 dots long. In this manual one dot length is also called one unit. Gap The silence between elements (1 unit), between characters (3 units) and between words (7 units). Koch method A way to learn: start with two characters at full speed, and add one character each time you copy 90 % of them right. Farnsworth timing Characters are sent at full speed, with longer gaps between characters and words, so the text arrives at a lower speed. QSO A radio contact between two stations. Over One station's turn to send in a QSO. Copy To receive Morse code and understand or write it down. CQ A general call: any station may answer. RST A signal report, such as 599. 5NN is 599 with the 9s sent as N. Prosign Two letters sent as one character, with no gap. This manual writes them in angle brackets, such as <AR>, <BK>, <KN> and <SK>. POTA, SOTA Parks on the Air and Summits on the Air: programs where an activator operates from a park or a summit and hunters contact the activator. P2P Park to park: a QSO between two activators. Pileup Several stations that call at the same time. Ragchew A long, chatty QSO. Fist How a person keys: their small timing errors. QRS, AGN, QRZ Please send slower; send again; who is calling me. TU, 73, 72 Thank you; best regards; best regards at low power (common in POTA). Sidetone The tone you hear while you key.

docs.title: Activate a park or summit
docs.text:
On this screen you are the activator on a park (POTA) or a summit (SOTA). You call CQ, a pileup of hunters answers, and you work the hunters one at a time. The device reads each over you send and answers the way hunters do on the air.

Open ON AIR in the menu, then POTA or SOTA. The header shows the program and the RCV, SND and VOL values.

Program QSOs for a valid activation You sign with POTA 10 72 SOTA 4 73

Set your callsign first in the CALLSIGN section of the settings. The hunters listen for it.

docs.title: Work a QSO
docs.text:
Your over ends one word gap after a last word of K, BK or KN, or when you stop keying for three word gaps. The footer tells you what to send next.

  1. Call CQ: CQ POTA DE <your call> K. With an empty pileup, one to three hunters call you. Each hunter sends its callsign once or twice.
  2. Send the callsign of one hunter, then a report: K1ABC 5NN. That hunter sends your report and its state, such as RR TU 559 CA CA 72. A hunter in Canada sends its province, such as ON. A hunter outside the US and Canada sends no state.
  3. Close the QSO: send TU, the hunter's state, and 72 or 73: TU CA 72 E E. To a hunter with no state, send TU 72 E E. The QSO goes in your log, and most hunters send E E or 73 E E back. Then the pileup calls again, and new hunters can join it.

The device counts a QSO as copied when your closing over holds the hunter's state. A QSO with a hunter that sends no state always counts as copied.

More ways to talk to the hunters:

You send The hunters do this Part of a callsign, such as K1A?, or a callsign with one character wrong The hunter whose callsign matches best sends its callsign twice. A callsign after your closing, such as TU CA 72 K2XYZ 5NN You close one QSO and start the next. CQ, QRZ or QRZ? The pileup calls again. CQ without your callsign A hunter asks CALL?. QRS The last transmission again, 4 WPM slower. Each QRS slows the hunters by 4 WPM more, down to 8 WPM, until the QSO ends. AGN, AGN? or ? The last transmission again. Anything else The hunter you work sends ?. With no hunter in a QSO, the pileup calls.

docs.title: What the screen shows
docs.text:
The transcript shows each over: YOU for yours, PILE for the pileup, and the hunter's callsign for the hunter you work. What the hunters send shows as a row of dashes until the QSO is in your log, so you copy it by ear. F3 (HINT) shows the text, and then reads HIDE.

Under the transcript:

Item What it shows NOW or LAST NOW during a QSO and before your first. LAST after a QSO: the items show the QSO you logged last. LOG QSOs in your log and the goal, such as LOG 3/10. The count turns green at the goal. GOOD QSOs where you sent the hunter's state back. CALL The callsign of the hunter. A green edge marks a QSO in progress. RST The report the hunter gave you. During a QSO, only HINT shows it. STATE The hunter's state or province, or DX for a hunter outside the US and Canada. During a QSO, only HINT shows it. After the QSO, the label is COPIED with a green edge, or MISSED with a red edge: whether you sent the state back. PILE How many hunters are in the pileup.

... marks an item with no value yet.

Under the items, your over shows as you key it. At the right of your over, the state shows LISTEN while the hunters send, YOUR TURN while they wait for you, and KEYING while you key. The footer shows the next step. With HINT on, the footer shows the exact text to send.

Band noise and fading play on this screen when you set them in the SOUND section of the settings.

docs.title: Pileup settings
docs.text:
The QSO section of the settings sets how the hunters behave. Their base speed is CHAR SPEED, with FARNSWORTH for longer gaps, in the RECEIVE section; MATCH uses your keyer speed.

Setting Values PILEUP OFF: one hunter at a time. TAKE TURNS: up to four hunters, who call one after another. OVERLAP: up to four hunters, who call at the same time. FIST HUMAN: each hunter keys with small timing errors. CLEAN: exact timing. SPEED SPREAD ON: each hunter sends up to 5 WPM faster or slower than the base speed.

Hunters send between 8 and 40 WPM. Each hunter sends at its own pitch, up to 200 Hz above or below your tone.

docs.title: Controls
docs.text:
Control Action F1 (SET) Stops the hunters and opens the settings at the QSO section. F4 (BACK) there returns, and the hunters send their last transmission again at the new settings. F2 (QRS) The same as sending QRS. F3 (HINT or HIDE) Shows or hides the hidden text and the exact next step. F4 (BACK) Pauses the activation and opens the ON AIR list of the menu. Click POTA or SOTA, or RESUME, to go on: the hunters send their last transmission again. The log stays while the device is on, until you start other practice. Dial turn Changes the focused header value. See Header values. Dial click Moves the focus to the next header value. Dial hold Turns the device off. Key Keys your over.

Each QSO in your log also counts in Progress.

docs.title: The controls
docs.text:
Control How you use it F1 to F4 The four buttons beside the screen, F1 at the top. Press a button and let go to use it. The column at the right edge, under the header, shows what each button does on the current screen. A blank label means the button does nothing there. F hold Keep an F button down for half a second. The button does its second action as soon as the half second ends, and nothing more when you let go. The small label in the button's box names the second action. A button with no second action does its usual action when you let go. Dial turn Turn the dial left or right. Hold it turned to step again and again. Dial click Press the dial and let go within 1 second. Dial hold Press the dial and keep it down for 1 second. This turns the device off on every screen after the boot screen. Key The paddle, straight key or sideswiper in the key jack. See Keys and jacks.

Each screen page in this manual has a table of what these controls do on that screen.

docs.title: Held buttons
docs.text:
Two held buttons work on every screen:

Hold Label Action F1 Set by F1 HOLD Does what F1 HOLD in the DEVICE section of the settings sets. The default is KEY OUT. F4 HOME Opens the KEYER screen. A drill or QSO you were in pauses: RESUME in the menu goes on with it.

On KEYER, F4 has no hold. With the memory row open, every hold sends its memory again and again instead. See Memories.

F1 HOLD has four values:

F1 HOLD Label Action KEY OUT KEYOUT Turns KEY OUT on or off. The status line shows KEY OUT ON or KEY OUT OFF. On a screen where your key does not key the radio, it shows KEY OUT ON: NOT ON THIS SCREEN. See The func jack. RESUME RESUME Goes on with the drill or QSO you paused. With nothing paused, it starts the last one you opened again. With no last one, the status line shows NOTHING TO RESUME. MEM ROW MEM Opens the KEYER screen with the memory row open. TIMING TIMING Opens the TIMING screen.

Some screens have more held buttons:

Screen Hold Label Action KEYER, memory row open F1 to F4 REPEAT Sends that memory again and again. See Memories. LETTERS F2 CLEAR Erases your letter statistics. See Letters. TIMING F2 CLEAR Clears the statistics and the tape. See Timing. Settings, editing a memory or your callsign F3 CLEAR Clears the text.

On every screen, your key sounds the sidetone and types or keys VBand over USB when USB OUT is TEXT or VBAND. On the KEYER, TIMING and RADIO screens, it also keys the func jack when KEY OUT is ON. The Key row of each table lists what else the key does on that screen.

docs.title: Turn on
docs.text:
Click the dial. The boot screen shows Morse code falling as rain in the colors of your palette. The rain builds your callsign in large letters. Then a line with the version and your callsign shows, and a list of startup checks, each marked as passed or failed.

To skip the boot screen, press any F button or turn the dial. The KEYER screen opens after the boot screen.

docs.title: Turn off
docs.text:
Hold the dial. After 1 second the status line says RELEASE TO POWER OFF. Let go of the dial, and the device saves everything and turns off.

To stay on, press an F button or turn the dial before you let go. The status line clears, and the button does nothing else.

If a save fails, the status line names what was not saved, and the device waits 3 seconds before it turns off.

When the battery is empty, the device saves everything and turns off by itself. See System.

docs.title: The screen
docs.text:
• The header across the top names the screen. It also shows details such as the keyer mode, the values the dial sets, and a battery icon at the right end. TX shows while your key keys the radio.
  • The column at the right edge, under the header, shows the labels of F1 to F4.
  • The footer at the bottom shows what the screen waits for or what the selected row does. Short messages show there for 5 seconds, brighter, and then the footer comes back. See Status messages.

docs.title: Header values
docs.text:
On every screen except KEYER, MENU and SETTINGS, the dial sets values that show at the right end of the header. Each screen shows the values it uses.

Value What it is Setting VOL 23 The volume. VOLUME in the SOUND section SND 20 Your keyer speed, in WPM. SPEED in the KEYER section RCV 20/15 The speed of what the device sends you: the character speed, then the Farnsworth speed. Equal numbers mean no Farnsworth spacing. CHAR SPEED and FARNSWORTH in the RECEIVE section
  • A dial click moves the focus to the next value. The focused number shows inverted. On RECEIVE KOCH, the focus also reaches LEVEL under the header.
  • A dial turn changes the focused value.
  • A dial turn does nothing while you key, and for one word gap after you stop. A brushed dial cannot change a value in the middle of your over.
  • Opening a screen puts the focus on RCV where it shows, on SND on TIMING, and on VOL on the others. After F1 (SET) and then F4 (BACK), the focus stays where it was.
  • With CHAR SPEED at MATCH, RCV shows your keyer speed. A turn sets CHAR SPEED, starting from that speed. To set MATCH again, use the RECEIVE section of the settings.
  • Turn the second RCV number down for Farnsworth spacing. Turn it up to the first number to stop the spacing.
  • On QSO and HUNT, a new RCV speed moves every station by the same amount: each keeps its offset from RCV and its fist. Any QRS ends.

docs.title: What the device saves
docs.text:
The device keeps everything below when it is off. It has no clock, so it does not keep the date or time.

What When it saves Settings 2 seconds after your last change. Memories When you leave the settings screen. Letter statistics and Koch level When you leave a receive drill or a ragchew. Progress of this session At most once a minute. Battery calibration When it changes. Settings, memories, letter statistics and progress When you turn the device off.

If the device loses power in another way, such as when you take the battery out, it can lose changes it did not save yet.

docs.title: Hunt
docs.text:
On this screen you are the hunter. An activator calls CQ from a park (POTA) or a summit (SOTA), you work the activator, and then you log the QSO. About two activators in three are on a park. An activator on a summit signs with /P after the callsign.

Open ON AIR in the menu, then HUNT. The header shows HUNT and the RCV, SND and VOL values. Set your callsign first in the CALLSIGN section of the settings.

docs.title: Work a QSO
docs.text:
Your over ends one word gap after a last word of K, BK or KN, or when you stop keying for three word gaps. The footer tells you what to send next.

  1. The activator calls CQ, such as CQ POTA DE K1ABC K1ABC K. While you are quiet, the activator calls again 3.5 seconds after each CQ. When you start to key, the CQs stop.
  2. Send your callsign. For a park to park QSO (P2P), send P2P, then your callsign. With HINT on, the footer shows both forms. The activator sends your callsign, your report and its state, such as K5XYZ GM UR 5NN CA CA BK. An activator in Canada sends its province, such as ON. An activator outside the US and Canada sends no state.
  3. Close the QSO: send TU, a report, your state and 72 or 73, such as TU 5NN TX 72. The activator says goodbye, such as TU 72 E E.
  4. Log the QSO: key the activator's callsign, without /P. The activator you logged shows in the items, and the next activator calls 1.5 seconds later.

The activator can copy your callsign wrong. This happens when you send a callsign with one character different from yours. The activator then sends that wrong callsign in its exchange. Send your callsign again before you close, and the activator sends the exchange again with your callsign. If you close with the wrong callsign, the QSO is busted.

More ways to talk to the activator:

You send The activator does this Part of your callsign, or any word with a digit, before the exchange Asks for it again, such as K5?. Anything else before the exchange QRZ? Your callsign, during the exchange Sends the exchange again with your callsign. Anything that does not close, during the exchange AGN? QRS The last transmission again, 4 WPM slower. Each QRS slows the activator by 4 WPM more, down to 8 WPM, until you log the QSO. AGN, AGN? or ? The last transmission again.

A closing over holds TU, 72, 73, 5NN, 599, TNX or RR.

docs.title: What the screen shows
docs.text:
The transcript shows each over: YOU for yours, THEM for the activator. What the activator sends shows as a row of dashes until you log the QSO, so you copy it by ear. F3 (HINT) shows the text, and then reads HIDE.

Under the transcript:

Item What it shows NOW or LAST NOW during a QSO and before your first. LAST after you log a QSO: the items show the QSO you logged last until the next activator answers you. HUNTED QSOs you logged. GOOD QSOs where you logged the activator's callsign right and the activator copied your callsign right. CALL The activator's callsign. After you log, the label says COPIED with a green edge, MISSED with a red edge when you keyed a wrong callsign, or BUSTED with a red edge when the activator copied your callsign wrong. RST The report the activator gave you. STATE The activator's state or province, or DX for an activator outside the US and Canada. FROM PARK, SUMMIT, or P2P for a park to park QSO.

During a QSO, only HINT shows the values of the items. ... marks an item with no value.

Under the items, your over shows as you key it. At the right of your over, the state shows LISTEN while the activator sends, YOUR TURN while it waits for you, and KEYING while you key. The footer shows the next step. With HINT on, the footer shows the exact text to send.

Band noise and fading play on this screen when you set them in the SOUND section of the settings.

docs.title: Settings
docs.text: The hunt uses CHAR SPEED and FARNSWORTH in the RECEIVE section of the settings, and FIST and SPEED SPREAD in the QSO section. PILEUP does not apply, because one activator calls at a time. The activator sends between 8 and 40 WPM, at a pitch up to 200 Hz above or below your tone.

docs.title: Controls
docs.text:
Control Action F1 (SET) Stops the activator and opens the settings at the QSO section. F4 (BACK) there returns. The activator calls CQ again, or during a QSO sends its last transmission again, at the new settings. F2 (QRS) The same as sending QRS. F3 (HINT or HIDE) Shows or hides the hidden text and the exact next step. F4 (BACK) Pauses the hunt and opens the ON AIR list of the menu. Click HUNT or RESUME to go on: the activator sends its last transmission again. The counts stay while the device is on, until you start other practice. Dial turn Changes the focused header value. See Header values. Dial click Moves the focus to the next header value. Dial hold Turns the device off. Key Keys your over.

Each QSO you log also counts in Progress.

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
This page installs PocketCW on a HamCube. An install writes the firmware, and when it needs it, the content pack with the words and voice before it. On Windows and Linux, you copy them to the device. On macOS, an install script does the copy, because macOS writes its own files to the device, and those files break the install.

PocketCW was tested on a Mini with board version 2.64. Other board versions and the Pro may work, but nobody has tried them yet.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• A computer with Windows, Linux, or macOS 10.15 or later on an Intel or Apple chip.
  • A USB cable that carries data. Some cables only charge. If the computer never finds the device, try a different cable.
  • About 10 minutes. The content pack is about 8 MB and takes several minutes to install.

docs.title: The content pack
docs.text:
The content pack holds the voice and the words for the drills. Install it:

  • on the first PocketCW install on a device. Without an F file first, a first install stops on the update screen.
  • when the device stays on the update screen after an install.
  • when the content pack changed since you last installed it. The notes of each release name the release that last changed it.
  • when NINJA or HEAD shows CONTENT PACK MISSING: INSTALL IT.

Otherwise, install the firmware alone.

If you might go back to the stock firmware, know this first: the content pack can write over the stock firmware's contact log, and that log is then lost. Where the stock firmware keeps its log is not known yet. A first install needs the content pack all the same.

docs.title: Is it safe?
docs.text:
The device has a small built-in program, the bootloader, that installs firmware. This install never touches the bootloader: PocketCW's files install after it, and the macOS install tool refuses any file that would write over it. If an install goes wrong, the bootloader still works, and you can run the install again.

To go back to the original firmware, see Go back to the stock firmware. That page installs the published stock version, V5.03. Some devices come from the factory with a newer, unpublished version, and the install replaces it for good. On board 2.64, V5.03 has no sound.

docs.title: Update mode
docs.text:
The device takes new firmware in update mode. To start update mode:

  1. Turn the device off, and unplug its USB cable. To turn it off, hold the dial down for about 2 seconds.
  2. Find F1 and F4. They are two of the four buttons beside the screen: F1 is the top one, and F4 is the bottom one.
  3. Hold F1 and F4 down.
  4. While you hold them, hold the dial down too.
  5. When the firmware update screen shows, let go of all three.

In update mode, the device shows up on the computer as a drive named POKEMON-2 or HAM MODULE. The drive holds one file, READY.TXT.

docs.title: Windows and Linux
docs.text:
Nobody has tested a Linux install yet. The bootloader needs the file's name to reach the drive before the file's data. Windows writes the name first. If a Linux install does not work, report it on the issue tracker.

  1. Download A000014.bin from the newest release. If you install the content pack, download F000400.bin too.
  2. Put the device in update mode.
  3. Plug the USB cable into the device and the computer. The drive opens.
  4. To install the content pack, copy F000400.bin to the drive. Wait until the drive closes and opens again with only READY.TXT. This can take several minutes. Then hold F4 to reset the drive. Without the content pack, go to step 5.
  5. Copy A000014.bin to the drive.
  6. Wait about 10 seconds. The drive closes, then opens again with only READY.TXT.
  7. Unplug the device, then click the dial to turn it on.

On Linux, run sync after each copy, so the file goes to the device at once.

If the drive holds a file other than READY.TXT before the copy, hold F4 to reset the drive.

docs.title: Start the script
docs.text:
1. Turn the device off, and unplug its USB cable.
  2. Open Terminal. Press Command and Space together, type Terminal, and press Return.
  3. Copy this line, paste it into the Terminal window, and press Return:
curl -fsSL https://kvmet.github.io/k5mme_pocketcw/install.sh | sh

The script downloads the newest PocketCW release and the install tool. It asks:

Install the content pack? [y/N]

Type y and press Return to install the content pack, then the firmware. Both install in one update mode session, so you put the device in update mode only once. Press Return alone to install only the firmware.

The script then says "Waiting for the device".

docs.title: Plug in the device
docs.text:
1. Put the device in update mode. If it already shows the firmware update screen, go to the next step.
  2. Plug the USB cable into the device and the Mac. After a few seconds, the script says "Found the device".
  3. macOS asks for your password. Type your Mac login password, and click OK. The install writes directly to the device, and macOS asks for your password before it allows that. macOS can ask again for the second file.

docs.title: Finish
docs.text:
The content pack takes several minutes, and the firmware about 10 seconds. The script shows this when the install works:

Finished. Unplug the device.
Then click the dial to turn it on.

Unplug the device, then click the dial to turn it on.

docs.title: While the install runs
docs.text:
• Do not unplug the device until the script says "Finished".
  • When the script finds a problem, it prints Problem: and the reason, then waits. Fix the cause, press Return, and follow the steps it prints again.
  • macOS can show a message about a disk it cannot read. Click Ignore. If you click Initialize by mistake, close the Disk Utility window that opens, and change nothing.
  • To stop the script at any time, press Control and C together.

docs.title: Check the version
docs.text:
On the KEYER screen, press F4 (MENU). Turn the dial to SYSTEM, and click the dial. The FIRMWARE row shows the version, such as v0.3.0.

If something goes wrong, see Troubleshooting.

docs.title: Release files
docs.text:
Each release has these files:

File What it is A000014.bin The firmware. F000400.bin The content pack: the words and voice for the drills, for the device's memory chip. When an install needs it, it installs before the firmware. See The content pack. pocketcw-flash The macOS install tool that the script runs. LICENSE The PocketCW license, GPL-3.0-or-later. B612-OFL.txt The license of the B612 Mono font. THIRD-PARTY.txt The licenses of the code libraries in the firmware, and the credits for the word list and voice in the content pack.

docs.title: Keyer
docs.text: The KEYER screen is the main screen. It opens after the boot screen. The header shows KEYER and the keyer mode.

docs.title: What the screen shows
docs.text:
Area What it shows Large digits Your sending speed in WPM, 5 to 60. TONE The sidetone pitch in Hz. VOL The volume, 0 to 44. 0 is off. OUT KEY OUT: ON when your key keys the func jack, OFF when it does not. While it is ON, the header shows TX. DIT The length of one dot at your speed, in milliseconds. Bar Your speed between 5 and 60 WPM. Timing tape Your keying drawn to scale. See below. Statistics line Your average gaps and speed. See below. Decode Four lines of what your keying decodes to.

A small mark under a value shows which value the dial sets: speed, volume or tone.

docs.title: Timing tape
docs.text:
The tape draws time from left to right, 4 pixels per dot length.

  • The KEY row shows the keyer output. In STRAIGHT mode, each mark has the color and shape of its timing grade.
  • The two rows under it show the two contacts of your key: DIT and DAH, or TIP and RNG in STRAIGHT mode. While both contacts are closed, a bar joins the two rows.
  • Under the rows, each decoded character shows under its marks.
  • Each gap between characters or words shows its length in units, in the color of its grade. A thin tick shows where the ideal gap would end.

A new page starts after a pause of 14 units or more, or when the next element would not fit.

docs.title: Timing grades
docs.text:
Every mark and gap gets a grade:

Grade Color Meaning Good Green Within 20 % of the ideal length. Off Amber Between good and bad. Bad Red More than halfway from the ideal length to the length where the decoder reads it as another kind, such as a dot read as a dash.

Each grade also has its own shape, so you can read the grades without color.

docs.title: Statistics line
docs.text: CHR and WRD are your average character gap and word gap in units (ideal: 3 and 7). RATIO is your average dash length over your average dot length (ideal: 3). The last value is the speed your timing works out to. Dashes in place of a value mean no data yet. Hold F2 (CLEAR) on the Timing screen to clear these statistics.

docs.title: Decode
docs.text: Each character has an underline in its grade: a thin line for good, a dashed line for off, a thick bar for bad. The grade is the worst timing in the character: its marks, its gaps, and the gap before it. * is a pattern that is not a character. A prosign shows as its two letters under a bar.

docs.title: Controls
docs.text: Control Action F1 (SET) Opens the settings at the KEYER section. F2 (MEM) Opens the memory row. See Memories. F3 (TMNG) Opens the TIMING screen. F3 hold (RADIO) Opens the RADIO screen, when the menu shows it. F4 (MENU) Opens the menu. Dial turn Changes the marked value: speed, volume or tone. A turn does nothing while you key, and for one word gap after you stop. Dial click Moves the mark to the next value: speed, then volume, then tone. Dial hold Turns the device off. Key Draws on the timing tape and decodes. Stops a memory that is sending.

docs.title: Keys and jacks
docs.text:
The device has two jacks for Morse. The key jack, labeled "key", takes your paddle or key. The func jack, labeled "func", keys a radio or an external keyer.

The USB port can also send your keying to a computer, as typed text or for VBand. See USB keyboard.

docs.title: Key types
docs.text:
Set the key type with MODE in the KEYER section of the settings. See Settings.

MODE Key How it keys IAMBIC A Dual-lever paddle One lever sends dots, the other dashes. Squeeze both levers and the keyer alternates dots and dashes. When you let go of both levers, the keyer stops after the element it is sending. IAMBIC B Dual-lever paddle The same as IAMBIC A, but when you let go of both levers after a squeeze, the keyer still sends the one element the squeeze asked for. This is the default. STRAIGHT Straight key The key closes the tip contact, and you time every element yourself. STRAIGHT Sideswiper Either side closes a contact, and either contact keys. You time every element yourself.

In both iambic modes, the keyer remembers a lever you press while it sends an element of the other kind, and sends that element next.

In the iambic modes, PADDLES sets which lever sends dots: NORMAL puts dots on the tip contact, and REVERSED puts dots on the ring contact. STRAIGHT mode ignores PADDLES.

docs.title: How the device reads your sending
docs.text:
• In the iambic modes, the keyer times every element at your set speed, so the decoder reads your sending at that speed.
  • In STRAIGHT mode, the decoder starts at your set speed and then follows the speed you actually send.

docs.title: The key jack
docs.text:
The key jack has two contacts, tip and ring.

  • A contact that is closed when you turn the device on does not key until it opens.
  • A ring contact closed for 5 seconds stops keying until it opens.
  • A tip contact closed for 30 seconds stops keying until it opens. This leaves time to hold a straight key down to tune a radio.

When a contact stops keying, the status line shows a message such as DAH STUCK ON: CHECK PLUG. In STRAIGHT mode the message names TIP or RNG (ring) instead of DIT or DAH.

A mono plug connects the ring contact all the time. Plug a mono plug in before you turn the device on: then the ring never keys, and the tip keys normally. If you plug a mono plug in while the device is on, the ring keys for 5 seconds before it stops.

docs.title: The func jack
docs.text:
The func jack keys a radio. It follows these settings in the KEYER section:

Setting Value What the func jack does KEY OUT ON Your key keys the func jack on the KEYER, TIMING and RADIO screens. The header of these screens shows TX. This is the default. KEY OUT OFF The func jack never closes. OUT TYPE STRAIGHT One line closes while the keyer sends, for a radio's straight key input. OUT LINES picks TIP KEYS or RING KEYS. OUT TYPE PADDLE Tip and ring follow your dot contact and your dash contact, for the radio's own keyer. OUT LINES picks DIT ON TIP or DIT ON RING.

Hold F1 to turn KEY OUT on and off from any screen, while F1 HOLD in the DEVICE section of the settings is KEY OUT, its default.

Only your own keying, your memories and a logging program over the serial port key the func jack. The practice screens and the settings never let your key key it, so a drill stays off the air. The stations of the practice screens never key it. A logging program keys it on every screen while KEY OUT is ON. Memories key the func jack only when KEY OUT is ON and OUT TYPE is STRAIGHT.

The LED lights while the keyer sends and while a memory sends.

docs.title: Letters
docs.text:
The LETTERS screen shows how well you copy each of the 44 Koch characters, and the characters you mix up most. The header shows LETTERS and your Koch level, such as LEVEL 12.

Open STATS in the menu, then LETTERS, or press F2 (LTRS) on the Progress screen.

docs.title: Where the numbers come from
docs.text:
Every character you copy in a receive drill or answer in a ragchew quiz counts. A character counts as right, as wrong (copied as another character), or as missed.

When a character reaches 200 tries, its counts halve. The numbers then follow how you copy now, more than how you copied long ago.

docs.title: What the screen shows
docs.text:
Each character has a tile, in the Koch order. A tile shows the character and the percent you copied right. The color of the tile shows how sure the device is that you know the character:

Color Meaning Green Known: the device is 95 % sure that you copy it at least 90 % right. Amber Not enough tries to tell. Red Weak: the device is 95 % sure that you copy it less than 90 % right. Gray, no percent Not sent yet.

Under the tiles, MIXUPS lists the six most common mixups, such as S/H 4X: the device sent S, you copied H, and this happened 4 times. Before your first mixup, the list says NONE YET: RUN A RECEIVE DRILL.

docs.title: Controls
docs.text: Control Action F1 (SET) Opens the settings at the RECEIVE section. F4 (BACK) there returns to this screen. F2 hold (CLEAR) Erases all counts and mixups. Your Koch level stays. F3 (KOCH) Goes on with the KOCH drill if it is paused, or starts it. F4 (BACK) Opens the STATS list of the menu. Dial turn Changes the focused header value. See Header values. Dial click Moves the focus to the next header value. Dial hold Turns the device off. Key Nothing more.

docs.title: Memories
docs.text:
The device stores four messages, M1 to M4. You key each message in once in the MEMORIES section of the settings. Then you send it with one press from the KEYER screen. Hold the button instead to send the memory again and again, for calling CQ until a station answers.

The first time PocketCW starts, the memories hold messages for a POTA activation with your callsign:

Memory Message M1 CQ POTA DE <your call> <your call> K M2 UR 5NN 5NN <BK> M3 TU 72 E E M4 QRZ DE <your call> K

docs.title: Send a memory
docs.text:
1. On the KEYER screen, press F2 (MEM). The memory row replaces the decode lines and shows each memory. The labels of F1 to F4 change to M1 to M4, and the footer says HOLD REPEATS CLICK CLOSES.
  2. Press F1 to F4 to send M1 to M4 once. Hold the button to send the memory again and again. An empty memory sends nothing, and the status line shows M1 IS EMPTY (SETTINGS).

The memory sends at your keyer speed and tone. The footer shows SENDING M1 KEY TO STOP. A held memory waits for the REPEAT EVERY time after it ends, then sends again. Between sends, the footer shows M1 REPEATS EVERY 6S KEY TO STOP.

With F1 HOLD set to MEM ROW, holding F1 on any screen opens the KEYER screen with the memory row open. See Held buttons.

A memory keys the func jack only when KEY OUT is ON and OUT TYPE is STRAIGHT. Otherwise the memory plays only as a tone, and the footer says why: M1 TONE ONLY: OUT TYPE PADDLE or M1 TONE ONLY: KEY OUT OFF.

docs.title: Stop a memory
docs.text:
Touch your key, press any F button, or leave the KEYER screen. While the memory row is closed, a dial click also stops the memory. An F button stops it as the button goes down, and does nothing else: press again to send a memory. A dial turn does not stop it.

Keying from a logging program over USB also stops a memory, so the two never key the radio together. A memory you send stops the program's keying.

docs.title: Controls with the memory row open
docs.text: Control Action F1 to F4 (M1 to M4) Sends that memory once. With AFTER SEND set to CLOSE, the memory row closes. While a memory sends, a press of any button only stops it. With the row open, the sending memory's button shows STOP; with the row closed, all four buttons show STOP. F1 to F4 hold (REPEAT) Sends that memory again and again, until you stop it. Dial turn Changes the marked value on the KEYER screen. Dial click Closes the memory row. While a memory sends, the click stops it instead. Dial hold Turns the device off. Key Stops a memory that is sending. With AFTER SEND set to CLOSE, the memory row closes.

docs.title: Edit the memories
docs.text:
Open the settings, and press F3 (NEXT) until the MEMORIES section shows. The section has six rows: M1 to M4, REPEAT EVERY and AFTER SEND. See MEMORIES for their values.

To edit a memory, select its row and click the dial. Then key the message. Click again to end. While you edit, the line under the list shows how many characters are left.

Control while you edit a memory Action F2 (DEL) Deletes the last character. A prosign goes as one character. F3 hold (CLEAR) Clears the memory. F4 (BACK) Leaves the settings. Dial turn Nothing. Dial click Ends editing. Dial hold Turns the device off. Key Adds what you key to the memory. A prosign goes in as <AR>. The memory gets one space between words, and no space at the start.
